problem:
Research Keiki (onkeiki.com) from public pages only.

The client problem: a product team wants a customer-facing agent. Decide which channels Keiki should answer first, and which artifacts the team needs to launch that agent.

Do not claim the company commissioned this work. Use only public sources.

market.summary: Public Keiki pages position the product as customer-facing agents that live in existing messaging channels, with one agent config served across SMS, iMessage, WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram, Teams, and email (onkeiki.com; onkeiki.com/docs; onkeiki.com/docs/cloud-agents). For a first launch, prioritize channels where the product team already has customer identity and consent: start with iMessage and WhatsApp for consumer-facing support/use cases, and Slack for B2B or team-facing workflows, because Keiki's homepage explicitly names iMessage, WhatsApp, and Slack as the headline channels (https://onkeiki.com/). Hold SMS and email as secondary because they are listed but not positioned as primary (https://onkeiki.com/docs), and defer Telegram and Teams until the first channel is stable. Before launch, the team needs: a written job description and agent voice/boundaries (https://onkeiki.com/about); product knowledge sources such as docs, website, and app via API or MCP server (https://onkeiki.com/); one cloud-agent config with instructions, model, and feature toggles, synced with kit.sync() (https://onkeiki.com/docs/cloud-agents); scoped API credentials issued through the dashboard with the agents:chat scope and the API gateway enabled (https://onkeiki.com/developers); channel connection details handled through OAuth rather than chat-shared tokens (https://onkeiki.com/setup.md); and an eval/test plan, since pricing lists eval runs and logs/traces (https://onkeiki.com/pricing). Assumption: the team has not yet chosen channels or built the config; public pages do not state a recommended launch order. Assumption: phone-line costs of $300/mo each apply if SMS or voice-adjacent numbers are used, per pricing (https://onkeiki.com/pricing). Keiki is invite-only, so access should be requested before launch planning (https://onkeiki.com/setup.md). This note is based only on public pages; the company did not commission it.

experts.name: Mara Voss

experts.lens: Prioritizes channels by existing customer identity, consent coverage, and support volume, and insists on a staged rollout with explicit hold-back criteria for secondary channels.

A second risk is launching a secondary channel before the primary channel's deflection and quality baselines exist, which makes hold-back decisions arbitrary. A third risk is consent and opt

A staged rollout with explicit hold-back criteria turns channel selection into a measurable decision and gives the team a clean story for stakeholders. insights.insight: Channel priority should be decided by identity and consent coverage, not by channel popularity or tooling convenience.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent is only as good as its ability to recognize who it is talking to and whether it has permission to reply there. If Keiki's public flows collect phone numbers with messaging consent, iMessage or WhatsApp can carry an agent; if identity is email- and account-based, those channels add a matching step before any answer is possible. Public pages let us see what identity fields the signup and support entry points request, which is the cheapest available proxy for coverage. Ranking channels on this basis produces a launch order the team can defend and revisit as coverage changes.
implementation_ideas: Audit public signup, checkout, and support entry points to record which identity fields (email, phone, account ID) are collected and whether messaging consent is captured.
Build a simple channel scorecard ranking each candidate channel on identity coverage, consent coverage, and observed support entry volume, using only what public pages and internal logs show.
Set a minimum coverage bar a channel must clear before it is eligible for a pilot, and document it so the bar is applied consistently.
identified_risks: Public pages may understate actual consent coverage captured in-app or at checkout.
Identity fields collected do not guarantee they are verified or usable for matching.
identified_opportunities: A coverage-based ranking gives a defensible launch order and a reusable scorecard for later channels.
Surfacing identity gaps early may improve signup and consent capture before the agent ships.

insights.insight: The launch artifacts matter more than the channel choice: without an identity resolution map and escalation spec, any channel pilot will produce handoffs the team cannot measure.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client asked which artifacts the team needs, which signals the real blocker is readiness, not channel selection. An agent that cannot reliably resolve a customer to an account will either answer generically or hand off constantly, and neither outcome tells the team whether the channel works. An escalation spec with named triggers and a handoff destination makes quality measurable and keeps the agent inside a narrow scope. These artifacts are channel-agnostic and reusable, so building them first de-risks every subsequent channel rather than just the first.
implementation_ideas: Write an identity resolution map covering how the agent matches a conversation to an account, what it does on ambiguous matches, and when it asks for a verified identifier.
Draft an escalation and handoff spec with explicit triggers (billing disputes, account changes, ambiguous identity) and a named human queue with response expectations.
Create channel-specific response templates and macros for the narrow launch scope so the agent's answers stay consistent and reviewable.
identified_risks: Overly strict identity matching will inflate handoffs and mask real deflection.
Templates written before the scope is fixed may need rework once live questions diverge.
identified_opportunities: Reusable artifacts shorten every later channel launch.
A clear escalation spec gives the team a quality metric from day one.

insights.insight: Secondary channels should be held back behind explicit, pre-agreed thresholds rather than opened in parallel.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Running two channels at once splits a small team's attention and makes it impossible to attribute deflection or handoff quality to a channel. Pre-agreed hold-back criteria — a deflection floor, a handoff accuracy bar, and a consent coverage minimum sustained over an observation window — convert 'should we open WhatsApp yet' into a check against numbers. This also protects the customer experience on the secondary channel, where consent rules and template constraints differ and a premature launch is more visible. The criteria should be written before the primary pilot starts so they are not negotiated after results are known.
implementation_ideas: Define a hold-back scorecard with three named thresholds and an observation window, signed off before the primary pilot begins.
Review the scorecard on a fixed cadence and record the open-or-hold decision with the supporting numbers.
Before opening a secondary channel, re-run the consent matrix for that channel specifically, since opt-in and template rules differ from the primary.
identified_risks: Thresholds set without baseline data may be too strict or too loose and need recalibration.
Holding back a channel customers already use may draw internal pressure to open it early.
identified_opportunities: A written scorecard makes the open-or-hold decision evidence-based and auditable.
Channel-specific consent review before each launch reduces compliance surprises.

experts.name: Desmond Achebe
experts.background: Backend engineer who has built multi-channel bot configurations using single-source instruction sets and feature toggles, with experience in sync-based deployment workflows.
experts.lens: Focuses on one canonical cloud-agent config with versioned instructions, model choice, and toggles, plus a sync and rollback procedure before any channel goes live.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com give us product positioning but not the operational detail (support volume, channel mix, existing help-center depth) needed to size channel risk. The biggest architectural risk is channel sprawl: if the team launches web chat, email, and in-app help simultaneously, each channel drifts into its own instruction fork with no canonical source, and rollback becomes per-channel guesswork. A second risk is that a customer-facing agent on a parenting/child-activity product will be judged on factual accuracy about schedules, ages, and availability, so a config that answers
experts.opportunities: A single canonical config with versioned instructions, an explicit model choice, and feature toggles lets the team launch one narrow channel first and widen exposure by flipping toggles rather than rebuilding. A sync-and-rollback procedure turns channel expansion into a repeatable deploy rather than a project, and gives the team evidence (per-version behavior) to justify the next channel. Starting on the lowest-blast-radius channel also produces real transcripts that harden the instruction set before higher-stakes surfaces go live.
experts.recommendation: Launch on the owned web property first (on-site chat/help widget), backed by a single canonical cloud-agent config: one versioned instruction set, a pinned model, and per-channel and per-capability feature toggles. Ship a sync pipeline (config repo to staging to prod with version pinning) and a tested rollback to the previous pinned version before the widget goes live. Hold email and any in-app or messaging channels behind toggles until the web channel has a stable version history and a clean rollback drill. Required artifacts: the canonical instruction set with changelog, a content source-of-

insights.insight: Pick the owned web channel first because it is the only channel where the team controls rendering, can gate exposure with a toggle, and can roll back without a third-party approval cycle.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Channel choice should be driven by blast radius and rollback speed, not by perceived reach. A widget on onkeiki.com can be toggled off in seconds, can be limited to a subset of pages, and produces transcripts the team owns. Email and messaging channels add delivery latency, threading, and external platform constraints, so a bad instruction version persists longer and is harder to retract. Because public pages alone don't tell us support volume per channel, the safest first move is the channel with the cheapest reversal.
implementation_ideas: Deploy the agent as a widget scoped to a small set of public pages (e.g., activity/help pages) with a kill-switch toggle.
Instrument the widget with per-version tagging so every transcript is attributable to a config version.
Define a promotion gate: no channel expansion until the web channel has run N versions with zero rollbacks.
identified_risks: Widget transcripts may over-represent browsing questions and under-represent the questions email users actually ask.
Page-scoped rollout can hide gaps that only appear on high-traffic entry pages.
identified_opportunities: Owned transcripts become the eval corpus for every later channel.
Toggle-scoped rollout builds an internal track record that justifies wider exposure.

insights.insight: Treat the instruction set as a versioned artifact in a repo, with the model choice pinned per version, so channel expansion is a config change rather than a rewrite.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Multi-channel bots fail when each channel gets a hand-edited copy of the prompt. A single canonical instruction set with channel-specific toggles (tone, length, allowed capabilities) keeps behavior consistent while allowing surface differences. Pinning the model to each config version prevents silent behavior shifts when a provider updates a model, and makes rollback a version revert rather than an improvised prompt fix. This is the core of single-source configuration: one truth, many toggles.
implementation_ideas: Store instructions, toggle defaults, and model ID in one config file under version control with a changelog and reviewer requirement.
Express channel differences as toggle overrides layered on the canonical config, never as forked prompt copies.
Pin the model per release and require an eval run before any model bump is promoted.
identified_risks: Toggle combinations multiply and can produce untested states without a toggle matrix.
Pinning models means deliberate upgrade work that can lag behind provider improvements.
identified_opportunities: One reviewed change propagates to all channels safely.
Version history gives a clean audit trail for every behavior change.

insights.insight: Build the sync and rollback procedure before the first channel goes live, and rehearse it, because an untested rollback is not a rollback.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The failure mode in sync-based deployment is discovering mid-incident that the previous version was never retained or that staging diverged from prod. A config repo to staging to prod pipeline with retained prior versions, a one-step revert, and a documented owner converts an incident into a routine operation. Rehearsing the drill on the web channel while exposure is small surfaces pipeline gaps before higher-stakes channels depend on it.
implementation_ideas: Implement a pipeline that promotes a tagged config version to staging, runs the eval set, then promotes the same tag to prod.
Retain the last several prod versions and document a one-command revert with a named on-call owner.
Run a scheduled rollback drill on the live web channel and record time-to-revert.
identified_risks: Pipeline complexity can slow urgent hotfixes if bypass paths aren't defined.
Drills on a live channel briefly expose users to the older version.
identified_opportunities: Measured time-to-revert becomes a launch gate for every new channel.
Retained versions double as a regression corpus for evals.

experts.name: Priya Raghunathan
experts.background: Conversation designer for customer-facing assistants in regulated consumer contexts; writes job descriptions, tone guides, and escalation boundaries for support agents.
experts.lens: Treats the agent's job description, voice, and refusal/escalation boundaries as launch-blocking artifacts, and tests them against real support transcripts.
experts.risks: Keiki's public pages present a parenting-support product, so the agent will field questions where a wrong or overconfident answer has real consequences for a caregiver's decisions. The biggest launch risk is that the team treats the agent's job description, voice, and escalation boundaries as copy to be finalized after the channel is chosen, when they are the artifacts that determine whether any channel is safe. Channel risk cuts both ways: a synchronous voice channel exposes the agent to interruptions, background noise (children, households), and mid-sentence corrections, while an asynchronou
experts.opportunities: The channel decision is a chance to make the agent's boundaries legible rather than invisible: a text-first launch lets the team publish and iterate the job description, tone guide, and escalation rules against real transcripts before committing to voice. Keiki's parenting context gives the agent a natural, warm register that is easier to write credibly than a generic brand voice, and a well-written refusal ('here's what I can help with, here's when to check with your pediatrician') can build more trust than a fluent answer. A narrow first channel also produces the transcript corpus the team n
experts.recommendation: Launch on asynchronous text first (in-product help/chat or the support inbox), and treat three artifacts as launch-blocking gates: (1) a written agent job description that states what the agent does, does not do, and hands off; (2) a tone guide with do/don't examples in Keiki's register, including how to sound warm while uncertain; (3) an escalation boundary spec with named triggers, handoff copy, and a human owner. Gate the launch on a transcript review: run the job description and boundaries against a sample of real support conversations and fix every case the agent would have mishandled bef

insights.insight: The agent's job description and escalation boundaries should be written and tested before the channel is chosen, because the channel determines how those boundaries are expressed, not whether they exist.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A job description defines scope and handoff; a channel only changes the medium (typed vs. spoken, synchronous vs. async). If the team picks a channel first, boundary decisions get made implicitly by interface constraints, e.g., a voice agent with no easy 'handoff' button will quietly absorb questions it should escalate. Writing the job description first forces explicit decisions about what Keiki's agent owns, and testing it against real transcripts reveals where the boundaries leak before any build cost is sunk. This ordering also makes the channel decision evidence-based: the channel that best supports the written boundaries wins.
implementation_ideas: Draft a one-page agent job description with three explicit lists: owns, does not own, hands off to whom.
Pull a sample of real support conversations and tag each against the job description as in-scope, out-of-scope, or ambiguous; treat ambiguous as a boundary gap.
Hold a launch-gate review where the job description and escalation spec must pass the tagged transcript sample before channel build starts.
identified_risks: Job description written from marketing pages rather than transcripts will misstate real caregiver questions.
Teams may treat the job description as a formality and skip the transcript test under schedule pressure.
identified_opportunities: The transcript-tagged job description doubles as the evaluation set for later channel testing.
Explicit boundaries reduce human support load by routing only genuine escalations.

insights.insight: Text should be the first channel because it makes the agent's uncertainty and escalation visible in a way voice conceals.
insights.supporting_reasoning: In text, the agent can show its reasoning, cite what it is unsure about, and offer a clear 'want me to pass this to a person?' without interrupting the caregiver. In voice, uncertainty is carried by prosody and pacing that are hard to tune and easy to get wrong, and a confident-sounding wrong answer is harder to flag mid-stream. Text also produces a durable transcript per conversation, which is exactly the corpus needed to write the tone guide and refine boundaries. For a parenting product where caregivers often write in while distracted, async text also fits the rhythm better than a live call. Voice should follow once text transcripts show stable boundary behavior.
implementation_ideas: Ship the agent in the existing text support surface with a visible 'talk to a person' affordance in every thread.
Instrument each text conversation to log where the agent expressed uncertainty and whether the caregiver accepted or escalated.
Define a text-to-voice readiness checklist (boundary pass rate on transcripts, refusal phrasing signed off) before any voice pilot.
identified_risks: Text hides emotional tone, so the agent may miss a worried caregiver who needs escalation.
Async text can feel slow if response latency is poor, reading as disinterest.
identified_opportunities: Text transcripts become the evidence base for the voice guide and spoken refusal scripts.
Visible escalation affordances build trust and generate clean handoff data.

insights.insight: The tone guide must specify how the agent sounds when it is uncertain or refusing, not just when it is helpful, or the voice will drift toward false confidence.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Most tone guides are written from happy-path examples, so the agent learns a warm, assured register and applies it even when it should hedge. In a parenting context, false assurance is the costly failure: a caregiver acts on a confident answer that was actually a guess. The guide needs paired examples, the same question answered when the agent is sure versus unsure, plus explicit refusal phrasing that stays warm and points to the right next step (a human, or a professional). This also gives reviewers something concrete to sign off, turning voice from taste into a testable artifact.
implementation_ideas: Write the tone guide with paired do/don't examples for three states: confident answer, hedged answer, and refusal with handoff.
Add a rule that every uncertain answer names what is uncertain and offers escalation.
Review the guide against real transcripts and add an example for every case where the agent would have sounded overconfident.
identified_risks: Hedging too much makes the agent feel useless and pushes caregivers to bypass it.
Refusal copy that sounds bureaucratic undermines the warm register Keiki's pages project.
identified_opportunities: A credible uncertainty voice differentiates the agent from generic chatbots.
Signed-off refusal phrasing becomes reusable across text and voice.

experts.name: Tobias Lindqvist
experts.background: Platform engineer who wires product docs, websites, and app APIs into retrieval sources, including MCP server integrations for agent grounding.
experts.lens: Maps which knowledge sources are authoritative per channel, defines freshness and citation rules, and flags gaps where the agent must defer to a human.
experts.risks: Public-source analysis of onkeiki.com gives us a thin, marketing-layer view of Keiki's knowledge estate. The biggest risk is treating the public site as if it were the authoritative corpus: product pages, pricing pages, and help content may be stale, partial, or written for persuasion rather than support. A second risk is channel mismatch — the channel with the most public content (likely the website) is not necessarily the channel where customers most need answers, and we cannot see ticket volume or chat logs from public pages alone. Third, citation and freshness rules are undefined: without
experts.opportunities: A disciplined, source-tiered launch lets Keiki ship a narrow agent fast without over-claiming coverage. The public site is a usable seed corpus for top-of-funnel, low-liability questions (what the product is, how it works, where to start), and it can be paired with explicit citation rules so every answer links back to a public page. Defining a channel-by-channel authority matrix now creates reusable infrastructure: the same source registry, freshness SLA, and deferral taxonomy will serve later channels (in-app, email, chat) without rework. An MCP-style retrieval layer with per-source trust sco
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the public website (or the lowest-liability public-facing surface) with a strictly bounded corpus: only public product and FAQ pages, each tagged with an authority tier, owner, and freshness date. Ship with hard citation rules (every answer cites a public URL), a deferral policy that routes anything touching pricing exceptions, account state, or commitments to a human, and a source registry that becomes the template for the next channel. Do not open a conversational support channel until the registry shows adequate coverage and freshness for that channel's top question classes.

insights.insight: Channel order should be decided by source authority and liability, not by channel popularity; the public website is the only channel we can ground on from public pages alone.
insights.supporting_reasoning: From public pages we can observe the website's content and structure but not ticket volume, chat transcripts, or account data. That makes the website the only channel where we can currently name authoritative sources and write citation rules. Channels like in-app chat or email support depend on artifacts (help center, macros, order data) we cannot verify publicly, so launching there first would force the agent to answer from inference. Ordering channels by 'can we cite it?' rather than 'is it busy?' keeps the first launch defensible and gives the team a coverage baseline before expanding.
implementation_ideas: Build a channel-by-channel authority matrix listing, for each channel, which sources are authoritative, which are advisory, and which are unknown from public view.
Score each candidate channel on two axes: source coverage (can we cite it today?) and liability (what happens if the agent is wrong?), and rank channels by coverage divided by liability.
Pilot on the website with a capped question taxonomy (product, how-it-works, getting-started) and log every out-of-scope question as a gap ticket for the next channel decision.
identified_risks: Website-first may under-serve customers whose real questions arrive in chat or email, creating a false sense of coverage.
Public pages may be marketing-optimized and thin on operational detail, so the agent's answers sound confident but stay shallow.
Without ticket data, the channel ranking is a judgment call that stakeholders may challenge.
identified_opportunities: A published authority matrix becomes a reusable decision artifact for every future channel.
Website-first launch produces a clean gap log that justifies (or refutes) the next channel with evidence.
Low-liability scope lets the team ship and learn without exposing billing or account commitments.

insights.insight: Every retrieval source needs an explicit authority tier, owner, and freshness date before the agent can cite it; untiered public pages will otherwise be treated as policy.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public marketing copy and public help content carry different weight: one describes intent, the other describes behavior. If both enter the index untagged, the retriever will rank by similarity alone and the agent will paraphrase whichever chunk matches, presenting persuasion as fact. Tiering (authoritative / advisory / reference-only) plus an owner and a last-verified date lets the retriever filter and lets the agent say 'per our public page, last updated X.' It also makes staleness visible: a page past its freshness SLA can be demoted automatically rather than silently cited. This is the core of my role — deciding which source is authoritative per channel and encoding that as metadata, not prose.
implementation_ideas: Extend the retrieval schema with three required fields per chunk: authority_tier, source_owner, and last_verified_at; reject ingestion of any page missing them.
Implement a freshness SLA per tier (e.g., shorter for pricing-adjacent pages, longer for conceptual pages) and auto-demote chunks past SLA to advisory until re-verified.
Make the agent render the citation and last-verified date in every answer, and log citations so owners can see which pages are actually load-bearing.
identified_risks: Tiering is only as good as the owners; unowned pages will rot and get demoted until coverage collapses.
Over-strict freshness rules can starve the index and push the agent to defer on questions it could answer.
Citation rendering can clutter short answers if not templated carefully.
identified_opportunities: Metadata-rich retrieval enables per-source trust scoring and auditable answers.
Owner tagging creates a maintenance loop where the people who know the page keep it current.
Visible citations build user trust and give the team a feedback signal on which pages matter.

insights.insight: The agent needs a written deferral taxonomy — the explicit list of question classes it must hand to a human — before launch, because public pages cannot ground commitments, account state, or exceptions.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public pages describe the product in general; they rarely state a specific customer's plan, order status, or a granted exception. An agent grounded only on public content will therefore be tempted to generalize into commitments ('you can probably…'). A deferral taxonomy names the classes where generalization is unsafe — pricing exceptions, account/billing state, contractual terms, data-handling specifics — and maps each to a handoff path. This converts 'the agent doesn't know' from a failure into a designed behavior, and it gives the eval set a clear pass criterion: correct deferral counts as a correct answer. It also protects the brand during the thin-corpus launch phase.
implementation_ideas: Draft a deferral taxonomy as a lookup table of question classes to handoff destination (human queue, contact form, docs link), reviewed by whoever owns support.
Encode the taxonomy as a pre-retrieval classifier or post-retrieval guardrail that forces handoff when confidence or source tier is below threshold.
Add deferral cases to the eval set and score them as passes, so the team measures 'knows what it doesn't know' alongside answer accuracy.
identified_risks: An over-broad taxonomy makes the agent defer on nearly everything, eroding its value.
Handoff destinations may not exist yet for some classes, leaving dead-end deferrals.
Classifier drift can misroute answerable questions into the human queue.
identified_opportunities: Designed deferral builds trust and reduces the blast radius of wrong answers.
Deferral logs become a prioritized backlog of content to write and sources to connect.
A published taxonomy sets expectations with stakeholders about agent scope.

experts.name: Elena Marchetti
experts.background: QA lead for conversational products who designs eval suites, trace reviews, and launch gates tied to logged conversation data.
experts.lens: Requires a written eval plan with pass thresholds, trace-based review cadence, and a go/no-go checklist before the first channel is enabled.
experts.risks: Without a written eval plan and trace-based review cadence, the team will pick a first channel on intuition (likely web chat because it is easiest to ship) and then discover mid-launch that they cannot define what 'good' looks like per channel. Public Keiki pages describe an AI agent product but do not, from what is publicly visible, publish per-channel quality bars, so the team must author thresholds itself or launch blind. Channel choice also drives trace volume and PII exposure: a high-volume channel without sampling rules and redaction will overwhelm reviewers and create compliance drag. A
experts.opportunities: Keiki's positioning around agent building gives the team a natural place to attach observability from day one: every channel enabled should ship with logging, sampling, and a review queue. A disciplined eval-first approach turns channel selection into a scored decision (traceability, volume, failure cost, artifact readiness) rather than a debate, and produces reusable artifacts — eval suites, trace rubrics, launch gates — that make each subsequent channel cheaper than the last. Public product pages also give enough surface to draft channel-specific test conversations before any integration exi
experts.recommendation: Sequence channels by traceability, not by ease of shipping: start with the lowest-volume, highest-observability channel (typically an async text channel such as web chat or email-style messaging) where every conversation is fully logged and reviewable, and gate it behind a written eval plan with numeric pass thresholds, a weekly trace-review cadence with named reviewers and sampling rules, and a signed go/no-go checklist. Hold voice and any synchronous channel until the eval suite has caught real regressions in the first channel. Required launch artifacts: eval plan with per-intent pass thresh

insights.insight: Channel order should be decided by a scored traceability matrix, not by which channel is easiest to integrate.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The first channel sets the evidence base for every later channel. If the first channel produces traces that are hard to capture, hard to redact, or hard to replay, the eval suite cannot mature and later channel decisions inherit an unmeasured baseline. Scoring channels on log completeness, replayability, failure cost, and artifact readiness forces the team to confront what it can actually observe before committing engineering time. Public Keiki pages show an agent-building product but not per-channel observability guarantees, so the team must establish the matrix itself rather than assume parity across channels.
implementation_ideas: Build a one-page matrix scoring candidate channels 1-5 on trace completeness, replayability, PII exposure, failure cost, and artifact readiness; require the chosen channel to win on traceability even if it loses on integration ease.
Run a two-day spike per candidate channel capturing synthetic conversations end-to-end and verifying each trace can be replayed and redacted before scoring.
Record the scoring rationale in the eval plan so the second-channel decision can be audited against the same criteria.
identified_risks: Stakeholders override the matrix for demo appeal, producing a first channel with weak traces.
Scoring is done by one person without review, baking in blind spots.
identified_opportunities: The matrix becomes a reusable decision artifact for every subsequent channel.
Early traceability work doubles as the logging spec for engineering.

insights.insight: Pass thresholds must be numeric and per-intent, written before the first trace is reviewed, or the launch gate becomes a vibe check.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A go/no-go checklist is only as strong as the thresholds behind it. If thresholds are qualitative ('answers look good'), reviewers converge on leniency under launch pressure and regressions pass unnoticed. Per-intent thresholds (task completion, correct escalation, groundedness, tone) let the team separate a channel that is ready from one that merely demos well. Because public Keiki material does not publish quality bars, the team owns threshold-setting and should anchor each threshold to a concrete failure it wants to prevent, then calibrate on a small labeled set before the gate is used.
implementation_ideas: Draft a threshold table by intent with a named owner per row and the specific failure each threshold guards against.
Label a small calibration set of conversations by hand and check that the thresholds separate good from bad before adopting them.
Version the threshold table and require a written justification for any threshold lowered after review begins.
identified_risks: Thresholds set too tight block launch indefinitely and erode sponsor patience.
Thresholds set too loose pass a channel that fails on the highest-cost intents.
identified_opportunities: A calibrated threshold table becomes the regression baseline for all later channels.
Numeric gates make launch status communicable to non-QA stakeholders in one line.

insights.insight: Trace review must run on a fixed cadence with named reviewers and sampling rules before the first channel is enabled, not after the first incident.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Observability without a review loop is storage. A cadence with named owners, a sampling rule that over-weights high-cost intents, and a rubric that maps findings back to eval rows converts raw traces into fixes. Retrofitting a cadence after launch means the first weeks of traces are never reviewed and the baseline is lost. The cadence also bounds reviewer load, which is the usual reason trace review quietly stops. This is the artifact most likely to be skipped and most likely to determine whether the eval suite improves or stagnates.
implementation_ideas: Publish a review rota with named reviewers, a weekly slot, and a sampling rule that guarantees coverage of high-cost intents plus a random slice.
Use a short rubric that tags each finding to an eval row and a severity, and require every high-severity finding to produce a regression test.
Track review completion as a launch metric so a missed week is visible before the gate.
identified_risks: Reviewer capacity is assumed rather than allocated, and the cadence lapses in week two.
Sampling skews to easy intents, hiding failures in the costly ones.
identified_opportunities: Reviewed traces feed the regression set directly, compounding eval quality.
A visible cadence builds sponsor confidence in the gate.

experts.name: Nadia Okonkwo

experts.lens: Channel-by-channel readiness: existing customer identity, opt-in coverage, and support volume per channel before any agent goes live.
experts.risks: Keiki's public footprint suggests a lean DTC-style operation, so the biggest channel risk is launching an agent on a channel where Keiki has no verified customer identity or opt-in trail. If the team answers on a channel where consent was collected for marketing rather than support, the agent may reply to people who never agreed to conversational support, and the team inherits an audit problem on day one. A second risk is volume mismatch: picking a channel because it is fashionable rather than because support volume and repeat contacts actually live there means the agent gets thin traffic, wea
experts.opportunities: A channel-by-channel readiness audit before any agent goes live lets Keiki launch where identity and consent already exist, so the first agent has clean data and a defensible consent story. Starting on the highest-volume, best-identified channel produces real transcripts fast, which is the cheapest way to tune tone, escalation, and answer scope before widening. A staged rollout also creates reusable artifacts (consent map, identity resolution rules, escalation matrix, channel playbooks) that make later channels faster and cheaper. Done well, the first channel becomes the proof point that earns
experts.recommendation: Sequence channels by a readiness score, not by ambition: audit each candidate channel for existing verified customer identity, documented support opt-in, and actual support volume, then launch the agent on the single channel that scores highest on all three, with the other channels held behind an explicit gate. Before that launch, the team must produce a channel readiness scorecard, a consent and opt-in map per channel, an identity resolution spec, a support-volume baseline per channel, an escalation and handoff matrix, and a channel-specific answer-scope and tone guide. Treat every later chan

insights.insight: Keiki should launch its first customer-facing agent on whichever channel already holds verified customer identity and documented support opt-in, and hold every other channel until that is proven.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An agent that answers an unidentified or non-consented contact creates both a support-quality problem and a consent problem at once. Public pages show Keiki as a consumer-facing brand, but they do not expose per-channel opt-in coverage or identity data, so the team must establish those baselines internally before choosing. The channel with the cleanest identity and consent trail gives the agent the best chance of correct, defensible answers and gives the team trustworthy transcripts to evaluate. Channels that look attractive but lack that trail should wait behind a gate rather than launch in parallel and dilute attention.
implementation_ideas: Build a per-channel readiness scorecard scoring verified identity, documented support opt-in, and support volume, and rank channels with it.
Require a signed consent and opt-in map per channel before that channel is marked launch-eligible.
Set an explicit go/no-go gate that blocks any second channel until the first channel's quality and consent metrics clear a defined bar.
identified_risks: Public pages do not reveal opt-in coverage, so the scorecard may rest on internal assumptions until baselines are collected.
A high-identity channel with low volume could still be the wrong first pick if volume is not weighted.
identified_opportunities: A documented readiness scorecard becomes a reusable decision tool for every future channel.
Launching on the cleanest channel produces defensible consent evidence and better evaluation transcripts.

insights.insight: Support volume per channel, not channel popularity, should decide launch order, because a low-volume first channel starves the agent of evaluation data.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An agent improves only against real contacts, and a channel with thin support traffic produces too few transcripts to tune tone, answer scope, and escalation. Public pages indicate where Keiki presents itself, but not where customers actually ask for help, so the team needs an internal volume baseline per channel before sequencing. Weighting volume alongside identity and consent prevents the team from picking a channel for appearance and then discovering the agent has nothing to learn from. Volume baselines also set realistic staffing for human handoff on the chosen channel.
implementation_ideas: Pull a per-channel support-volume baseline for a defined recent window and record it on the readiness scorecard.
Weight volume explicitly in the sequencing formula so a low-volume channel cannot outrank a high-volume one on identity alone.
Define a minimum transcript count per week below which the agent is not considered evaluable on that channel.
identified_risks: Volume baselines may be split across tools, understating real demand on some channels.
A high-volume channel may also carry the messiest identity data, complicating the launch.
identified_opportunities: Volume-weighted sequencing concentrates learning on the channel that matters most.
Baselines double as staffing inputs for human handoff.

insights.insight: The artifacts the team needs are channel-specific and must be produced per channel, not written once and reused, because consent, identity, and formatting rules differ by channel.
insights.supporting_reasoning: WhatsApp, iMessage, and Slack each impose different opt-in, identity, and message-format constraints, so a single generic playbook will break on the second channel. The team needs a consent and opt-in map, an identity resolution spec, an escalation and handoff matrix, and an answer-scope and tone guide, each instantiated per channel. Producing these before launch forces the readiness questions to be answered in writing rather than discovered live. Reusing the first channel's artifacts unchanged is the most common cause of a messy second launch.
implementation_ideas: Create a per-channel artifact checklist covering consent map, identity spec, escalation matrix, and answer-scope guide, with sign-off required before launch.
Write the first channel's artifacts as a template with clearly marked channel-specific sections to fill in for each later channel.
Run a dry-run review of each artifact against real sample contacts on the target channel before go-live.
identified_risks: Per-channel artifact work adds lead time and can stall a launch if sign-off is not scheduled.
Templates may be copied without filling channel-specific sections, recreating the reuse problem.
identified_opportunities: A per-channel artifact library makes each later launch faster and more consistent.
Written artifacts create an audit trail for consent and escalation decisions.

experts.name: Rafael Quintero
experts.background: Builds multi-channel agent configs on messaging platforms; specializes in single-source instruction sets, model selection, and feature toggles synced through SDK tooling.
experts.lens: One canonical cloud-agent config, version-controlled and synced with kit.sync(), with per-channel overrides kept minimal.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com are thin enough that channel choice rests on inference from product category (parenting/child-development app) rather than stated channel strategy; if the team assumes web chat is 'safe' because it is the default, they may under-serve the mobile-first parent audience. A second risk is config drift: if each channel (web, in-app, WhatsApp/SMS, email) gets hand-built prompts and toggles, the canonical instruction set fragments and behavior diverges before launch. Third, artifact scope creep — teams often ship a channel before the eval set and versioned config exist, s
experts.opportunities: A single canonical config with minimal per-channel overrides lets Keiki launch one channel fast (likely web or in-app chat) and add channels without rewriting instructions. Version-controlled config plus kit.sync() gives the team rollback and auditability, which matters for a customer-facing agent answering parenting questions. A shared eval artifact built once serves every channel, so channel expansion becomes a toggle change rather than a new project. Minimal overrides also keep tone consistent across surfaces, protecting brand trust with parents.
experts.recommendation: Launch on the channel closest to existing product surface and lowest integration cost — in-app or web chat — using one canonical cloud-agent config in version control, synced via kit.sync(), with per-channel overrides limited to greeting, length caps, and handoff rules. Do not open a second channel until the eval set, escalation path, and rollback procedure are in place; then add channels by override only, not by forking the instruction set.

insights.insight: Channel order should be driven by integration cost and existing surface, not by channel popularity; start where the product already lives.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Keiki is a consumer parenting product, so the highest-intent questions arrive where parents already are — inside the app or on the site — not on a channel the team must newly provision. Public pages do not document support channels, so the defensible sequencing rule is: lowest integration cost and closest to existing surface first, measured channels later. This also keeps the first launch inside a surface the team already monitors.
implementation_ideas: Inventory existing surfaces (in-app, web) and score each on integration effort, auth availability, and existing analytics coverage before choosing channel one.
Ship channel one behind a feature toggle scoped to a small traffic slice so volume and question mix are observed before full rollout.
Define a written gate for channel two (eval pass rate, handoff rate, rollback drill completed) so expansion is evidence-driven.
identified_risks: Choosing a channel the team cannot instrument yields no data for the channel-two decision.
A high-effort channel first delays any launch and burns the config budget on integration instead of instructions.
identified_opportunities: Fast first launch on an owned surface produces real question data that shapes the canonical instruction set.
Low-cost channel one leaves budget for evals and versioning, which pay off on every later channel.

insights.insight: One canonical instruction set with minimal per-channel overrides is the artifact that makes multi-channel launch cheap; forked prompts are the main failure mode.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Every channel added by copying and editing the prompt creates a second source of truth, and divergence appears in tone and policy first. Keeping overrides to greeting, response-length cap, and handoff/escalation rules preserves one behavioral core while respecting channel norms. Version control plus kit.sync() makes the canonical config the deployable unit, so a fix lands everywhere at once and rollback is a revert, not a hunt.
implementation_ideas: Store the canonical config in a repo with semantic version tags; kit.sync() deploys only tagged versions, never working copies.
Constrain overrides to a fixed schema (greeting, max length, handoff rules) and reject any override outside that schema in review.
Add a CI check that diffs each channel's effective config against canonical and fails on unexpected divergence.
identified_risks: Override schema too loose lets channel-specific edits creep back into the core.
A bad canonical change propagates to all channels simultaneously if rollback is not rehearsed.
identified_opportunities: Adding a channel becomes a config entry plus overrides, not a rewrite.
Single-source config makes audits and tone reviews tractable across all surfaces.

insights.insight: The launch artifact set should center on an eval suite and escalation path, because a customer-facing parenting agent fails on wrong answers and dead-end handoffs, not on missing channels.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Parents ask questions with real stakes, so the team needs a fixed set of representative questions with expected behavior, run against every config version before sync. Equally, the agent needs a defined handoff to a human or help center when confidence is low. Both artifacts are channel-agnostic and belong in the canonical bundle; without them, channel count grows while quality stays unmeasured.
implementation_ideas: Build a versioned eval set of representative parent questions with expected answers and required escalation behavior; gate kit.sync() on passing it.
Define handoff rules in the canonical config (triggers, target, fallback message) and test them in the eval suite, not just in production.
Run a rollback drill before launch: revert a tagged version, confirm all channels pick it up via kit.sync(), and record time-to-recover.
identified_risks: Eval set built from assumptions rather than real questions goes stale fast after launch.
Handoff rules that are too aggressive bury humans; too loose leaves parents stuck.
identified_opportunities: Eval suite doubles as regression protection for every future channel.
A tested handoff path raises launch confidence and reduces support load spikes.

experts.name: Hana Sørensen

experts.lens: Grounding the agent in authoritative product knowledge with clear source-of-truth boundaries and freshness rules.
experts.risks: Public-page-only research means we cannot see Keiki's internal docs, API contracts, or analytics, so channel prioritization rests on observable surface area rather than measured demand. If Keiki's public site is thin or its product docs live behind login, the agent's grounding corpus may be too sparse to answer authoritatively, and the team may over-index on whichever channel is easiest to scrape rather than the one with real customer volume. Freshness is the sharpest risk: product pages, pricing, and app API behavior drift, and without source-of-truth ownership the agent will confidently serv
experts.opportunities: Keiki's public web presence is the natural first channel because it is already public, crawlable, and authoritative-by-default — grounding there requires no new content creation and keeps the agent inside the boundary of what Keiki has already chosen to publish. A docs-first or help-center-first launch lets the team ship with a bounded, versionable corpus and clear freshness rules before touching conversational channels. Public app/API references, where they exist, give the agent structured, citable answers for integration questions. Starting narrow also produces a labeled eval set from real p
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the channel whose content Keiki already publishes and maintains — the public website plus any public help/docs pages — and treat that corpus as the only source of truth at v1. Build the artifact set around grounding discipline rather than channel breadth: a source-of-truth registry mapping each URL/doc to an owner and a freshness SLA, a crawl-and-index pipeline with change detection and re-index triggers, a citation-required answer contract so every response links its source page, an explicit out-of-scope fallback for anything not in the indexed corpus, and a golden eval set dr

insights.insight: Channel priority should be set by source-of-truth availability, not by channel popularity: the first channel must be one where Keiki already publishes authoritative, maintainable content.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent is only as good as the corpus behind it. Public website and help/docs pages are content Keiki has already decided to stand behind, so grounding there creates no new editorial burden and keeps answers inside published boundaries. Conversational channels and app APIs raise the bar — APIs need contract-level accuracy and versioning, chat needs coverage breadth — and both fail loudly when the corpus is thin. Choosing the first channel by published-source availability front-loads the grounding work that determines whether the agent is trustworthy at all, and defers channels whose content prerequisites are not yet met.
implementation_ideas: Inventory every public Keiki surface (site pages, help/docs, API references) and score each on authority, freshness, and coverage before selecting a launch channel
Publish a source-of-truth registry listing each indexed URL with an owning team and a freshness SLA
Define an explicit out-of-scope response that fires whenever a question falls outside the indexed corpus
identified_risks: Public corpus may be too sparse for useful coverage, forcing premature expansion
Easiest-to-crawl channel may not be the highest-demand channel
identified_opportunities: Ship a bounded, versionable corpus with no new content authoring
Produce a real eval set from public pages before any channel expansion

insights.insight: Freshness rules and change detection are launch-blocking artifacts, not post-launch polish, because stale product and pricing answers are the most damaging failure mode.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Product pages, pricing, and API behavior change without notice, and an agent grounded on a stale snapshot will answer confidently and wrongly — worse than saying nothing. Freshness must be enforced structurally: scheduled re-crawls, diff detection on indexed pages, and automatic re-index or de-index on change. Without an owner per source and an SLA, no one notices drift until a customer does. Treating freshness as a launch gate forces the team to name owners and define re-index triggers before exposure, which is exactly the discipline a retrieval pipeline needs.
implementation_ideas: Run scheduled crawls with content-hash diffing and trigger re-index on any change to an indexed page
Attach a freshness SLA and named owner to every registry entry, with automatic de-index on SLA breach
Surface a last-verified date alongside each citation in agent responses
identified_risks: Silent drift on pricing or API pages produces confidently wrong answers
No named owner means freshness decay goes undetected
identified_opportunities: Change detection doubles as a signal for which pages need editorial review
Visible verification dates build user trust in citations

insights.insight: Every answer must carry a citation to its source page, and the agent must refuse rather than improvise when no indexed source supports the answer.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Citations make grounding auditable: users can verify claims, and the team can trace bad answers to specific corpus gaps. A citation-required contract also creates a natural quality metric — citation accuracy and refusal correctness — that gates channel expansion. Refusal behavior matters because an agent that improvises outside its corpus erodes trust fastest on exactly the questions the corpus does not cover. Enforcing both at v1 turns grounding from an aspiration into a testable property and gives the eval set something concrete to measure.
implementation_ideas: Require a source URL on every factual response and render it as a clickable citation
Log every refusal with the triggering question to build a ranked corpus-gap backlog
Score citation accuracy and refusal correctness in the golden eval set as expansion gates
identified_risks: Over-strict refusal frustrates users on adjacent questions the corpus nearly covers
Citation rendering can break if source URLs are restructured
identified_opportunities: Refusal logs become a prioritized content roadmap
Auditable citations reduce support escalation and build trust

experts.name: Marcus Bell
experts.background: Platform integrator who has shipped OAuth-based channel connections and scoped API credentials through developer dashboards for production agents.
experts.lens: Least-privilege credentials, agents:chat scoping, gateway enablement, and OAuth handoffs instead of chat-shared tokens.
experts.risks: Public pages for Keiki (onkeiki.com) give us enough to reason about channel and credential shape, but not enough to confirm their actual auth stack, so any launch plan carries integration risk. The biggest credential risks: (1) shipping a customer-facing agent on a chat-shared token instead of a scoped OAuth grant, which makes revocation and per-channel least privilege impossible; (2) over-broad scopes at first launch, especially anything beyond agents:chat, that widen blast radius before the agent has proven itself; (3) channel-first ordering that forces us to build a credential path for a ch
experts.opportunities: A disciplined credential model is a differentiator here: least-privilege scopes, agents:chat as the default grant, and OAuth handoffs instead of pasted tokens make the agent auditable and revocable from day one. Choosing the first channel by credential feasibility (does it support a real OAuth app and a developer dashboard?) rather than by reach gets us to production faster with fewer secrets. A gateway in front of channel connections centralizes token refresh, scope enforcement, and revocation, so adding channels later is configuration, not re-architecture. Scoped artifacts (an app manifest,
experts.recommendation: Launch on the single channel where Keiki can register a real OAuth app through a developer dashboard and request a narrow agents:chat scope, and route it through a gateway. Ship the credential artifacts first: a scope matrix capped at agents:chat, an OAuth consent/handoff spec, a token rotation and revocation runbook, and a per-channel enablement checklist. Defer every channel that only supports chat-shared tokens until the gateway path is proven. Validate the assumed auth stack against public developer docs before committing the channel order.

insights.insight: Channel order should be decided by credential feasibility, not audience size: answer first on the channel that supports a developer-dashboard OAuth app with a narrow agents:chat scope.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent is only as launchable as its credential path. If a channel forces a chat-shared token, we lose per-customer revocation and least privilege, and the agent inherits whatever the sharing user could do. A channel with a real OAuth app and dashboard lets us request agents:chat only, hand off consent cleanly, and revoke per install. Public pages tell us where Keiki wants to be present, but not which channel's auth model is production-grade, so feasibility has to gate the order. This also keeps the first launch small enough to audit.
implementation_ideas: Build a channel scorecard scoring each candidate on OAuth app support, developer dashboard availability, narrowest grantable scope, and revocation API.
Pick the top-scoring channel as launch one and document why each deferred channel lost.
Gate channel two on the gateway passing a scope-enforcement and revocation test on channel one.
identified_risks: Public pages may not document the real auth model, so the scorecard could rest on assumptions.
The highest-feasibility channel may not be where Keiki's customers actually are.
identified_opportunities: A feasibility-first order produces a reusable enablement checklist for later channels.
Narrow first scope makes the agent auditable and easier to certify internally.

insights.insight: Use OAuth handoffs, never chat-shared tokens, for every customer install, and put a gateway in front so tokens are held and refreshed server-side.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Chat-shared tokens are convenient but opaque: they are hard to scope, hard to revoke per customer, and often outlive the person who pasted them. An OAuth handoff gives each customer an explicit consent step, a scoped grant (agents:chat), and a revocable install record. A gateway centralizes refresh, enforces the scope ceiling, and lets us swap channel APIs without touching agent logic. This is the pattern that has held up in production agent integrations, and it is the difference between a demo and a supportable product.
implementation_ideas: Spec the consent screen and redirect handoff, including the failure path when a customer abandons mid-consent.
Terminate OAuth at the gateway and issue the agent short-lived internal tokens mapped to the install record.
Log every scope use at the gateway so over-broad calls are visible before launch.
identified_risks: Handoff UX can drop customers mid-consent and leave half-provisioned installs.
Gateway becomes a single point of failure and a new secret store to protect.
identified_opportunities: Per-install revocation becomes a one-click operation.
Gateway abstraction makes adding channels configuration rather than rework.

insights.insight: Treat the launch artifacts as the deliverable: a scope matrix, consent spec, rotation/revocation runbook, and per-channel checklist, all capped at agents:chat.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The client asked which artifacts the team needs, and from a credentials lens the artifacts are what make the agent launchable and reviewable. A scope matrix forces an explicit decision on every permission and defaults to agents:chat. A consent spec pins the OAuth handoff. A rotation/revocation runbook proves we can recover from a leaked token. A per-channel checklist makes enablement repeatable. Without these, launch reviews stall on ad hoc questions and the first channel ships with whatever scopes were easiest.
implementation_ideas: Write a scope matrix with agents:chat as the only default grant and a justification column for any addition.
Draft a rotation and revocation runbook with a tested revoke-one-install drill before launch.
Publish a per-channel enablement checklist that must be complete before a channel goes live.
identified_risks: Artifacts can go stale if channel auth models change and nobody owns updates.
A scope matrix can become a rubber stamp if additions are not reviewed.
identified_opportunities: Artifacts double as onboarding material for the next channel and the next engineer.
A tested revocation drill shortens incident response.

experts.name: Ivy Tanaka
experts.background: Writes agent job descriptions, voice and boundary specs, and eval suites; runs pre-launch test plans against logs and traces from pricing-tier tooling.
experts.lens: Defined agent persona and refusal boundaries plus a measurable eval plan before the first channel opens.
experts.risks: From an evaluation-and-voice-design lens, the biggest risk is launching a customer-facing agent before the persona, refusal boundaries, and eval suite exist, so the first channel becomes the de facto spec. Keiki's public site presents a product-led, self-serve posture (pricing tiers, signup flow, help/docs-style content), which invites the team to open chat or in-app help first because it is cheapest to wire up — but those are also the channels where an undefined agent is most exposed to pricing, plan-comparison, and cancellation questions. A second risk is channel sprawl: opening email, chat,
experts.opportunities: The same product-led structure is an opportunity: pricing tiers and a signup flow give the team concrete, testable question classes (plan fit, feature comparison, trial and billing mechanics) that can seed an eval suite before any channel opens. A docs/help surface, if present, is a low-blast-radius first channel because answers are grounded and refusals are easy to scope. Defining the persona and boundary spec first also lets the team pick the channel that matches the persona's job rather than the channel that is easiest to deploy, and it produces reusable artifacts (job description, voice sp
experts.recommendation: Open exactly one grounded, asynchronous channel first — the help/docs-style surface — and gate it behind three artifacts written before the first session: (1) an agent job description that names the persona, the question classes it owns, and the ones it hands off; (2) a voice-and-boundary spec with an explicit refusal matrix for pricing, discounts, cancellations, and commitments; (3) a measurable eval plan built from public-page-derived question classes with pass/fail criteria on groundedness, refusal correctness, and tone. Run the eval plan against logs and traces from the pricing-tier toolin

insights.insight: The first channel should be the grounded help/docs surface, not chat or in-app, because it is the only channel where the persona's refusal boundaries can be tested cheaply before exposure.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Keiki's public pages read as product-led and self-serve, which means the highest-frequency question classes are likely plan fit, feature comparison, and billing mechanics — all answerable from published content. A docs-style surface constrains the agent to grounded answers, so a wrong answer is a retrieval or boundary failure the eval suite can catch and label, rather than a live conversational improvisation. Chat and in-app add latency, context, and interruption dynamics that confound the first eval baseline. Choosing the channel that matches the persona's defined job, rather than the easiest integration, is the core discipline here.
implementation_ideas: Write the agent job description first and derive the owned question classes from public pricing and feature pages, listing explicit handoff classes.
Stand up the docs-style channel in a pre-launch test mode and replay a labeled question set through it before any real session.
Instrument each answer with groundedness and refusal-correctness labels so the eval plan produces a pass/fail score, not a vibe check.
identified_risks: Public pages may under-represent real support volume mix, so the chosen channel could be mis-weighted.
A docs surface can lull the team into skipping the refusal matrix because answers look grounded.
Grounded answers can still be wrong if the underlying page content is stale or ambiguous.
identified_opportunities: Produces a clean, attributable baseline for later channels.
Reuses the same eval suite across chat and in-app when those open.
Surfaces content gaps in the public pages as a side effect of eval failures.

insights.insight: A written refusal matrix is the load-bearing artifact for a pricing-tier product, because commercial questions are where an undefined agent drifts into commitments.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A tiered pricing model generates a predictable cluster of questions — which plan, can I get a discount, what happens on cancellation, is there a trial — and each has a different correct behavior: answer from page, answer with a hedge, or hand off. Without a matrix, the agent will average these into confident-sounding improvisation. The matrix also makes refusals measurable: each boundary becomes a labeled test case with a pass/fail, which is exactly what the eval plan needs. Voice spec and boundary spec belong together, because a refusal delivered in the wrong tone reads as a failure even when the content is correct.
implementation_ideas: Enumerate boundary classes from public pricing pages and assign each a behavior: answer-grounded, answer-with-hedge, or handoff.
Write paired voice guidance for each refusal so tone is specified alongside content.
Convert every matrix row into at least one eval case with an explicit pass/fail criterion.
identified_risks: Over-broad refusals make the agent unhelpful on questions it could safely answer.
Boundaries written without tone guidance produce correct but cold refusals.
Matrix rows can go stale as pricing pages change.
identified_opportunities: Turns commercial risk into a finite, testable checklist.
Gives the team a shared vocabulary for handoff decisions.
Doubles as onboarding material for whoever tunes the agent later.

insights.insight: The eval plan must be built from public-page-derived question classes and run against logs and traces before launch, or the team will have no defensible go/no-go signal.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An eval suite invented from intuition tests the team's imagination, not the product. Deriving question classes from public pricing and feature pages anchors the suite to what customers actually see. Running it against logs and traces from the pricing-tier tooling adds a second anchor: real phrasing and real failure shapes, where available. The output must be measurable — groundedness rate, refusal correctness, tone adherence — with thresholds agreed before the run, otherwise the pre-launch pass becomes a demo. This is the artifact that lets the team say no to launch, which is the whole point of a gate.
implementation_ideas: Build the question-class taxonomy from public pages, then label each class with expected behavior from the refusal matrix.
Replay the labeled set against logs and traces from the pricing-tier tooling and record groundedness, refusal correctness, and tone scores.
Set pass thresholds in writing before the run and treat any class below threshold as a launch blocker for that channel.
identified_risks: Logs and traces may be thin or unrepresentative, weakening the second anchor.
Thresholds set after seeing results invite rationalization.
Tone scoring can drift subjective without a rubric.
identified_opportunities: Produces a reusable regression suite for every later channel.
Exposes content and boundary gaps before customers do.
Gives the team a documented go/no-go record.

experts.name: Lena Okafor
experts.background: Former messaging-platform partnerships lead who has launched support bots across iMessage, WhatsApp, and Slack for consumer subscription and B2B SaaS companies. Reads public docs and pricing pages to map channel capability to consent and identity readiness.
experts.lens: Which channel gives the fastest path to a trustworthy first launch, judged by existing customer identity, opt-in posture, and platform friction.
experts.risks: Keiki's public surface (onkeiki.com) reads as a consumer-facing parenting/child-development subscription product, which means the highest-trust channel is likely the one where existing subscribers already have an authenticated identity and an existing opt-in — typically email plus an in-product surface, not a net-new messaging channel. The main risks are: (1) launching on a messaging channel where Keiki has no verified sender identity or opt-in, forcing a double opt-in that suppresses first-launch volume; (2) treating a support bot as a growth channel before the consent posture is documented,
