Both carry existing identity and an existing opt-in, and both avoid app-store review. That gives the team a low-friction first launch to prove answer quality, escalation, and handoff before touching a messaging platform. A second-wave opportunity is a single messaging channel chosen by observed inbound volume rather than by platform popularity — if support requests already arrive via a channel, the opt-in
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the authenticated in-product/web help surface, backed by the existing transactional email stream, and defer all messaging channels to a second wave gated on evidence. Concretely: ship a scoped agent that answers only from approved public/help content, identifies the user from the existing session or email token, and escalates anything account-specific to a human. Before any messaging launch, produce four artifacts: (1) a channel scorecard ranking candidates by existing identity, existing opt-in, and platform friction; (2) a consent and identity map showing how each channel hand

insights.insight: The trustworthy first launch is the channel Keiki already authenticates, not a messaging platform.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A first launch is judged on whether the agent can reliably know who it is talking to and whether that person already agreed to hear from Keiki. An authenticated in-product or logged-in web surface satisfies both by construction: the session supplies identity and the user initiated the interaction. Transactional email tied to the subscription carries a weaker but existing relationship and a verified address. Messaging channels require a new sender identity, business verification, and a fresh opt-in, all of which add friction and failure modes before the team has proven answer quality. Public pages show Keiki sells a subscription, so subscriber records and email addresses exist; they do not show any messaging presence, so we cannot assume one.
implementation_ideas: Stand up the agent behind the existing logged-in help entry point so identity comes from the session, with a read-only account summary passed to the agent.
Wire the transactional email stream to offer an agent handoff on reply, using the verified sender address as the identity key.
Scope v1 answers to approved help and public content only, with a visible 'talk to a human' path on every response.
identified_risks: Session-based identity may not cover pre-purchase or logged-out visitors, splitting the experience.
Email replies can arrive from aliases or shared inboxes, weakening the identity join.
Approved content may be thin, producing frequent escalations that look like agent failure.
identified_opportunities: Proves answer quality and escalation before any platform review cycle.
Builds the identity and consent map that every later channel reuses.
Creates a clean baseline of support volume for measuring the pilot.

insights.insight: Channel choice should be driven by observed inbound volume and existing opt-in, not by which platform is fashionable.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The fastest path to trust is a channel where customers already contact Keiki, because the opt-in and identity work is largely done and the agent meets users where they already are. Picking a channel by popularity forces the team to manufacture demand and consent simultaneously. Since public pages do not disclose Keiki's support channels, the team must derive this from internal ticket and contact data, then rank candidates on three axes: existing identity join, existing opt-in evidence, and platform friction such as verification and template approval. The winning channel is the one that scores well on all three, which is usually the one already generating inbound.
implementation_ideas: Build a channel scorecard scoring each candidate 1-5 on identity join, opt-in evidence, and platform friction, and require internal data to fill it.
Sample the last quarter of inbound contacts by channel to identify where users already initiate conversations.
Pilot only on the top-scoring channel, capped to a defined user segment and time box.
identified_risks: Internal inbound data may be too sparse to rank channels confidently.
A high-volume channel can still have poor identity join, producing wrong-account answers.
Pilot scope creep if the scorecard is treated as a formality.
identified_opportunities: Avoids building on a channel customers do not use.
Surfaces consent gaps early, before engineering spend.
Produces a defensible, evidence-based channel decision for stakeholders.

insights.insight: The artifacts that matter most are the consent-and-identity map and the answer-boundary spec, not the bot framework.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Most first-launch failures are not model failures; they are identity and consent failures. An agent that answers account questions for the wrong person, or messages someone who never opted in, loses trust faster than a slightly weaker model. A consent-and-identity map forces the team to state, per channel, how a handle joins to the subscriber record and what opt-in evidence exists, which exposes gaps before launch. An answer-boundary spec defines what the agent may answer, what it must escalate, and the human-handoff SLA, which keeps the blast radius small. Both artifacts are cheap, channel-agnostic, and reusable, so they compound across every later launch.
implementation_ideas: Write a one-page consent-and-identity map per candidate channel listing the identity key, join method, opt-in evidence, and fallback when the join fails.
Write an answer-boundary spec with an explicit allow list, escalate list, and a human-handoff SLA, signed off by support.
Add a pre-launch checklist that blocks any channel launch until both artifacts are complete and reviewed.
identified_risks: Artifacts can go stale as channels or consent rules change.
Sign-off can bottleneck if support is not resourced to review.
A map that looks complete can hide a weak join the team has not tested.
identified_opportunities: Reusable across every future channel, cutting later launch time.
Makes consent gaps visible to legal and support early.
Gives a clear escalation contract that protects trust.

experts.name: Diego Salcedo
experts.background: Backend engineer who has shipped LLM agents on managed platforms, working with cloud-agent configs, MCP servers, and scoped API credentials. Focuses on reproducible config sync and least-privilege access.
experts.lens: What must exist in the config, credentials, and knowledge-source wiring before an agent can answer safely in production.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com give us marketing copy, not a contract. Before any agent answers a customer, the config must pin down: which channels are actually live and supportable (web chat widget, email, in-app help, WhatsApp/SMS, social DMs), what identity/auth model each channel uses, which knowledge sources are authoritative and versioned, and which credentials are scoped per channel. The biggest config risk is channel sprawl: launching on every channel at once multiplies auth surfaces, rate limits, and failure modes before the knowledge base is proven. Second risk: knowledge-source wirin
experts.opportunities: A narrow first channel (likely the owned web chat or in-app help, where the team controls the widget, auth context, and logging) lets the team ship with least-privilege credentials, full transcript capture, and a fast rollback. That same channel produces the eval data needed before opening email or messaging channels, which have asynchronous SLAs and weaker identity signals. Scoped, per-channel service credentials and a versioned knowledge snapshot give reproducible config sync, so every answer can be traced to a config commit and a knowledge version. A staging channel mirroring production let
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the single owned channel with the strongest identity and logging story (web chat or in-app help), backed by a versioned knowledge snapshot, per-channel scoped credentials in a secrets manager, a staging mirror, and a transcript-plus-eval harness. Treat email and messaging channels as phase two, gated on measured answer quality and a documented escalation path. Confirm the actual live channels from the product itself, not just the public site, before finalizing the config.

insights.insight: Channel choice must be driven by identity and logging capability, not by where marketing copy points.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent's safety depends on knowing who it is talking to and being able to replay what it said. Owned web/in-app channels usually carry session identity and full transcript capture; email and social DMs arrive with weak identity and asynchronous SLAs. Public pages tell us positioning, not which channels are instrumented. So the config should encode a channel capability matrix (identity source, auth method, rate limit, transcript store, escalation hook) and the first launch should pick the channel that scores highest on that matrix.
implementation_ideas: Build a channel capability matrix as a config file: identity source, auth method, rate limits, transcript retention, escalation webhook per channel.
Gate channel enablement in config behind a flag that requires a populated matrix row and a passing staging eval.
Log every answer with channel ID, config commit hash, and knowledge version for replay.
identified_risks: Public pages may list channels the product does not actually support or instrument.
Weak-identity channels invite account-specific answers the agent cannot verify.
identified_opportunities: Owned channel gives full-fidelity eval data before opening harder channels.
Capability matrix becomes reusable config for future channels.

insights.insight: Knowledge sources must be versioned and pinned per deploy, or answers are not reproducible.
insights.supporting_reasoning: If the agent retrieves from live CMS pages or a shared drive, the same question can get different answers across deploys with no record of why. A bad answer becomes undebuggable. Pinning a knowledge snapshot hash into the agent config, and recording that hash with every transcript, makes each answer traceable to an exact knowledge state. This is the config-sync discipline that separates a demo from a production agent.
implementation_ideas: Snapshot the approved knowledge base at deploy time and store the snapshot hash in the agent config.
Record the snapshot hash alongside every transcript entry.
Add a config check that blocks deploy if the knowledge snapshot is older than a set threshold or unapproved.
identified_risks: Stale snapshots produce confidently wrong answers after product changes.
Unapproved sources (drafts, internal docs) leak into customer answers.
identified_opportunities: Reproducible bad-answer replay shortens debugging.
Snapshot approval becomes a lightweight content-review gate.

insights.insight: Credentials should be scoped per channel and per environment, never shared.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A single broad key across channels and environments means one leak or one bad deploy reaches everything. Per-channel, per-environment service credentials in a secrets manager limit blast radius and make revocation surgical. The config should reference credential handles, not raw keys, so config sync stays reproducible without secrets in the repo. Least privilege also constrains what the agent can do on each channel (read vs. write, which APIs).
implementation_ideas: Store credentials in a secrets manager and reference handles only in config.
Issue separate credentials per channel and per environment with minimum scopes.
Add a rotation runbook and a config lint that fails on inline secrets.
identified_risks: Handle drift between config and secrets manager breaks deploys silently.
Over-broad scopes creep back in without a lint.
identified_opportunities: Surgical revocation limits incident blast radius.
Scoped credentials double as an audit trail of agent capabilities.

experts.name: Amara Chen
experts.role: Conversation designer and brand voice lead
experts.background: UX writer who drafts agent job descriptions, tone guides, escalation boundaries, and refusal patterns for customer-facing assistants. Treats the job description as a launch artifact, not a nice-to-have.
experts.lens: Whether the agent's scope, voice, and handoff rules are written down and testable before any channel goes live.
experts.risks: Without a published, testable job description, Keiki's first channel choice will be driven by product convenience rather than by where the agent's scope can actually be bounded. Public marketing pages typically show the happy-path story and hide the messy edges (refunds, plan changes, account recovery, out-of-scope questions), so a team can go live on a high-traffic channel with no written refusal patterns or escalation boundaries. Voice drift is the second risk: if tone guidance lives in a slide deck instead of a launch artifact, each writer and each channel will improvise a different Keiki.
experts.opportunities: Writing the job description first turns channel selection into a scoping exercise: the channel where the agent's allowed intents, refusal patterns, and escalation triggers can be enumerated and tested wins the launch slot. A written tone guide and refusal library become reusable assets across every later channel and double as onboarding material for human agents who inherit escalations. Treating the job description as a launch artifact also gives the product team a reviewable object that design, support, and legal can sign off on before any channel goes live, which shortens the path to a defen
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the single lowest-risk, highest-scriptability channel that Keiki's public pages imply (a written/async surface such as web chat or a contact form over voice), and gate the launch on four artifacts being written and testable: (1) an agent job description listing in-scope intents, out-of-scope intents, and explicit refusal patterns; (2) a tone and voice guide with do/don't examples; (3) escalation boundaries with named triggers and a human handoff script; (4) a test script that exercises each refusal and escalation path before go-live. No channel goes live until all four exist an

insights.insight: Channel order should be decided by scriptability, not traffic: the first channel must be one where the agent's allowed intents and refusal patterns can be fully enumerated and tested.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A job description is only testable if the surface constrains what can arrive. Async written channels let the team capture every intent class, write a refusal for each out-of-scope case, and replay test scripts deterministically; real-time voice adds latency, interruption, and repair moves that multiply the untested surface. Since public pages show what Keiki offers but not the full support tail, the team should pick the channel with the smallest unknown tail first and expand only after the refusal library holds.
implementation_ideas: Score each candidate channel on intent predictability, async vs real-time, and ease of replaying test scripts; pick the top scorer as launch channel one.
Write the job description's out-of-scope list per channel before writing any prompt or flow.
Define a channel-expansion gate: a new channel opens only when the existing refusal library covers its top intent classes.
identified_risks: Product pressure to launch on the highest-traffic channel before the refusal library is complete.
Voice launched first with no written repair or interruption patterns.
identified_opportunities: A scriptable first channel produces a reusable refusal library that de-risks every later channel.
Channel scoring gives the product team an objective, reviewable decision record.

insights.insight: The job description, tone guide, and escalation boundaries must be written as launch artifacts with owners and sign-off, or they will degrade into informal guidance nobody tests.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Artifacts without an owner and a review step are drafts forever. Making the job description a gated launch artifact forces the team to name who approves scope changes, who owns the tone guide, and what triggers escalation, so QA can test against a fixed document instead of a moving one. This mirrors how a human hire's role is defined before day one: scope, voice, and handoff are agreed in writing, then performance is measured against them.
implementation_ideas: Create a one-page agent job description template with fields for in-scope intents, out-of-scope intents, refusal patterns, escalation triggers, and named approver.
Attach a tone guide with paired do/don't example responses for each intent class.
Add a pre-launch checklist that blocks go-live until each artifact has an owner and a recorded sign-off.
identified_risks: Artifacts written once and never updated as scope drifts.
No named owner means no one notices when the agent answers outside its written scope.
identified_opportunities: Signed artifacts double as onboarding material for human agents receiving escalations.
A fixed document makes regression testing of voice and refusals possible.

insights.insight: Escalation boundaries and refusal patterns are the highest-value part of the job description because they define what the agent will not do, and they must be tested before launch, not after.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Customers judge an assistant most harshly at the edges: the question it should have handed off and the answer it should have declined. Public pages rarely document those edges, so the team must invent and write them. A refusal pattern per out-of-scope class plus a named escalation trigger per risky intent gives QA concrete cases to run; without them, the first edge case is discovered in production by a customer, and the handoff script is improvised in the moment.
implementation_ideas: Write a refusal pattern for every out-of-scope intent class, each with one example response in Keiki's voice.
Define escalation triggers as named conditions (e.g., billing dispute, account recovery, explicit request for a human) with a fixed handoff script.
Build a pre-launch test script that runs every refusal and escalation case and records pass/fail before go-live.
identified_risks: Refusals written in a flat tone that reads as a dead end rather than a handoff.
Escalation triggers too vague to test, so QA passes cases that should fail.
identified_opportunities: A tested refusal library reduces silent wrong answers at the edges.
Named triggers make handoff quality measurable after launch.

experts.name: Ravi Menon
experts.background: QA and ML-eval specialist who builds test suites and trace reviews for support agents, using eval runs and logs to gate releases.
experts.lens: What evidence proves the agent is ready, and which artifacts capture pass criteria, regression cases, and trace review before launch.
experts.risks: Public pages alone give me almost no ground truth on Keiki's actual support volume, ticket taxonomy, or channel mix, so any channel-first decision is inference from marketing copy and site structure rather than measured data. Without baseline transcripts, we cannot build a regression set that reflects real user phrasing, and the first eval run will be scored against synthetic cases we wrote ourselves. Keiki's public surface appears to be a content/booking-style site, which means the highest-value questions may be pre-purchase and content-navigation questions where a wrong answer is cheap but a
experts.opportunities: A narrow, low-blast-radius first channel lets us stand up the full eval and observability loop cheaply: a golden set, a rubric, trace capture, and a release gate, all before touching a higher-stakes channel. Public pages give us a legitimate seed corpus for the golden set (FAQs, product/content descriptions, navigation intents) that we can label and version without inventing customers. If we treat the first channel as a pilot with explicit pass criteria, the artifacts produced (regression cases, trace review notes, scored eval runs) become the evidence base for expanding to the next channel an
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the lowest-stakes, highest-volume-by-inference channel: asynchronous web/on-site chat or a contact-form-style assistant scoped to content and pre-purchase questions, explicitly excluding anything transactional or account-specific. Gate the launch on a versioned artifact set: (1) a golden eval set seeded from public pages plus labeled paraphrases, (2) a written pass-criteria rubric with numeric thresholds per intent class, (3) trace logging with span capture and a sampled trace-review checklist, and (4) a regression suite that every prompt/model change must pass. Do not expand t

insights.insight: The first channel should be chosen by blast radius and reviewability, not by guessed volume, because public data cannot rank channels reliably.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Keiki's public pages show a content-and-booking-style surface but no ticket counts or channel mix, so volume is an assumption. What we can observe is recoverability: an async web chat answer that is wrong can be corrected in-thread or escalated, and every exchange is text we can log and review. A live phone or synchronous channel compresses the review window and hides reasoning. Choosing on blast radius means the eval gate is meaningful from day one because failures are cheap and fully traceable, and the channel decision itself becomes revisitable once real volume data arrives.
implementation_ideas: Score candidate channels on a simple matrix: recoverability of a wrong answer, availability of a text transcript, and whether the intent is pre- or post-purchase.
Scope the pilot agent's intent allowlist to content and pre-purchase questions and hard-refuse account/transactional intents with a handoff message.
Instrument the pilot channel with full trace capture from the first session so the channel choice can be re-evaluated against real volume.
identified_risks: Volume assumptions baked into the pilot may misallocate effort if the real traffic sits elsewhere.
An allowlist that is too narrow makes the agent look unhelpful and depresses adoption, muddying the eval signal.
identified_opportunities: A recoverable, fully logged channel produces clean training and regression data fast.
The channel-scoring matrix becomes a reusable artifact for the next channel decision.

insights.insight: Pass criteria must be written and versioned before the first eval run, or the gate will drift to whatever the agent happens to score.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Without a pre-registered rubric, thresholds get set post hoc and every run 'passes'. The rubric needs per-intent-class criteria (correctness against source, groundedness, refusal behavior, handoff correctness, tone) with numeric thresholds and a defined sample size, plus a rule for what counts as a blocking failure. Because we are seeding from public pages, the rubric must also require citation to a public source for factual claims, which is checkable in a trace. Pre-registration is what turns an eval run into evidence rather than a demo.
implementation_ideas: Write a rubric file in the repo with per-intent criteria, thresholds, sample sizes, and a blocking-failure list; require a PR review to change it.
Require every factual answer in an eval trace to carry a source citation that a reviewer can check against the public page.
Tag each eval run with the rubric version and model/prompt version so scores are comparable across runs.
identified_risks: Thresholds set without baseline data may be arbitrary and either too lax or unachievable.
Reviewers may grade inconsistently without a calibration step.
identified_opportunities: A versioned rubric makes launch decisions auditable and defensible to the product team.
Citation requirements double as a groundedness check that catches hallucination early.

insights.insight: Trace review is the artifact most likely to be skipped and most likely to catch the failures evals miss, so it needs its own sampled checklist and severity taxonomy.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Golden-set evals test what we thought to write; trace review tests what actually happened, including multi-turn drift, silent handoff failures, and confident wrong answers on intents we never enumerated. Public-only research makes this gap larger because our seed cases come from marketing language, not real phrasing. A sampled review with a fixed checklist and severity levels (blocking, major, minor) converts raw logs into a regression backlog, and any unresolved blocking class becomes a launch blocker. Without it, the eval suite ossifies around our assumptions.
implementation_ideas: Define a trace-review checklist with severity levels and a fixed sample rate per eval cycle, reviewed by someone other than the prompt author.
Convert every blocking or major trace finding into a named regression case added to the suite before the next run.
Hold a short trace-review readout before each release decision, with unresolved blocking classes listed explicitly.
identified_risks: Sampling bias if reviews only pull easy or short traces.
Reviewer time is scarce and the checklist can decay into box-ticking.
identified_opportunities: Trace findings feed the regression suite directly, closing the loop between observation and test coverage.
A severity taxonomy gives the product team a shared language for launch readiness.

experts.name: Sofia Brandt
experts.role: Launch program manager for customer-facing AI
experts.background: Program manager who sequences multi-channel agent rollouts, coordinating legal, support, and engineering around consent, OAuth setup, and staged exposure.
experts.lens: Sequencing and dependencies: which channel ships first, what is deferred, and which artifacts must be signed off before exposure widens.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com give us little verified detail on Keiki's actual channel mix, support volume, or existing consent and OAuth posture, so any sequencing plan rests on assumptions the team must confirm. A customer-facing agent on an unproven channel can expose the brand before legal sign-off on consent language and data handling exists. OAuth setup for any channel that touches a customer's account or calendar is a hard dependency that can silently slip and block launch. If we widen exposure across channels simultaneously, support and engineering absorb parallel failure modes with no
experts.opportunities: Sequencing lets us ship one low-blast-radius channel first to generate real transcripts that harden the agent before wider exposure. A staged rollout creates natural checkpoints where legal, support, and engineering each sign off on a defined artifact set rather than a vague go/no-go. Deferring high-dependency channels (those needing OAuth or account linking) until the consent and auth artifacts are signed reduces rework. Each channel we defer is a chance to reuse the same consent, escalation, and fallback artifacts, so the second launch is cheaper than the first.
experts.recommendation: Ship a single low-dependency, read-mostly channel first — most likely a web or in-product help surface where the agent answers from public/approved content with a clean handoff to human support — and defer any channel requiring OAuth or account access until a signed artifact pack exists. Gate widening on a fixed checklist: approved consent and privacy copy, OAuth scopes and token-handling review, escalation and fallback runbook, support staffing sign-off, and a rollback/kill-switch procedure. Only after the first channel's transcripts and defect log are reviewed do we open the next channel, re

insights.insight: Sequence channels by dependency weight, not by customer demand: the first channel should be the one with the fewest auth and consent prerequisites.
insights.supporting_reasoning: The binding constraint on a customer-facing agent is not model quality but the artifacts that must be signed before exposure. Channels that require OAuth or account linking carry more sign-off surface (scopes, token storage, revocation) than a read-only help surface. Shipping the low-dependency channel first produces real usage evidence that de-risks the higher-dependency channel, and it lets legal review consent language against actual behavior rather than a spec. Because public pages don't confirm Keiki's channel mix, the team must validate which channel truly has the lowest dependency weight before committing.
implementation_ideas: Score each candidate channel on a simple dependency matrix: auth required, consent copy needed, platform review needed, human-handoff complexity.
Pick the lowest-scoring channel as launch one and document why each other channel is deferred.
Set an explicit trigger (e.g., N reviewed transcripts and zero open severity-1 defects) that must be met before the next channel opens.
identified_risks: Lowest-dependency channel may also be lowest-value, producing weak evidence.
Dependency scoring done on assumptions rather than verified platform requirements.
identified_opportunities: Real transcripts from launch one harden the agent and the consent copy before higher-risk exposure.
A documented deferral rationale makes the sequencing defensible to legal and support.

insights.insight: The launch artifact pack — consent copy, OAuth scope review, escalation runbook, support sign-off, kill switch — is the real gate, and it must be signed before any exposure widens.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent fails launch reviews on missing artifacts, not on missing features. Each artifact maps to a stakeholder who must own it: legal owns consent and privacy copy, engineering owns OAuth scopes and token handling, support owns the escalation and fallback runbook and staffing, and the program owns the rollback procedure. Treating these as a single signed pack with named owners converts a fuzzy go/no-go into a checklist with accountable signatures. Since we only have public pages, the pack must be drafted from first principles and validated with each owner rather than assumed to exist.
implementation_ideas: Build a one-page artifact checklist with a named owner and sign-off date per item, reviewed in a single cross-functional gate meeting.
Require the kill-switch and rollback procedure to be demonstrated, not just documented, before widening.
Version the artifact pack so each new channel reuses signed items and only adds channel-specific deltas.
identified_risks: Owners sign off on paper without testing the runbook or kill switch.
Consent copy approved for one channel is reused where it doesn't legally fit.
identified_opportunities: A reusable signed pack makes the second and third channel launches materially faster.
Clear ownership reduces late-stage legal and support surprises.

insights.insight: Deferring OAuth-dependent channels is a feature of the plan, not a delay: it protects the first launch from auth slippage and lets us reuse artifacts once auth is proven.
insights.supporting_reasoning: OAuth setup is the most common silent blocker: scope review, token storage, and revocation behavior each need engineering and often legal input, and any slip cascades into the launch date. By explicitly deferring auth-dependent channels, the first launch date stops depending on the slowest dependency. When those channels do open, they inherit the already-signed consent, escalation, and rollback artifacts, so the marginal sign-off is only the auth-specific delta. The tradeoff is that account-aware experiences arrive later, which the team should communicate up front.
implementation_ideas: Publish a channel roadmap that names the deferred auth-dependent channels and the artifact that unblocks each.
Run OAuth scope review in parallel with launch one so the deferral is short, not open-ended.
Define the minimum auth-specific artifact delta so the second launch reuses the signed pack rather than restarting review.
identified_risks: Deferral stretches long enough that stakeholders perceive the program as stalled.
Auth scope creep during parallel review reopens already-signed artifacts.
identified_opportunities: First launch date decouples from the slowest auth dependency.
Second launch is cheaper because it reuses the signed artifact pack.

experts.name: Corinne Adeyemi
experts.background: Former messaging-platform product lead who has launched support agents across iMessage and WhatsApp for consumer subscription apps; writes channel-priority frameworks grounded in consent and identity coverage.
experts.lens: Which channel has verified customer identity and existing opt-in, and which channels are merely listed in docs versus actually positioned as primary.
experts.risks: Public pages for Keiki (onkeiki.com) are likely to show channel presence (a contact form, maybe a mailto, possibly social handles) without revealing which channels carry verified identity or a real opt-in. The core risk is that the team treats a listed channel as a launch-ready channel. A contact form or generic support email is a documented artifact, not a consented, identity-verified conversation surface. Launching an agent there first means the agent answers anonymous or semi-anonymous traffic with no reliable way to tie a conversation to an account, plan, or subscription state. Secondary r
experts.opportunities: The same constraint is the opportunity. Public pages give a cheap, honest inventory of what Keiki already publishes as a contact path, and that inventory can be sorted by identity and consent rather than by novelty. If Keiki already runs an owned, logged-in surface (account area, in-app help, or a help center tied to sign-in), that is the natural first channel: identity is verified by session, consent is implied by the customer initiating inside the product, and the agent can read subscription state. A public web form or email is a fine second channel for pre-sale and top-of-funnel questions,
experts.recommendation: Answer first on the single channel where Keiki already has verified identity and an existing opt-in — most plausibly an owned, signed-in surface (in-product help or an authenticated help center) if the public pages confirm one exists; otherwise the owned web contact form, scoped narrowly to triage. Do not launch on WhatsApp or iMessage first unless public pages show Keiki already collecting a messaging opt-in. Before build, produce four artifacts: (1) a channel-priority matrix scoring every publicly listed channel on identity coverage, consent status, and whether it is documented versus actual

insights.insight: Separate 'listed' from 'operated': a channel named on Keiki's public pages is a documentation fact, not evidence of consent, identity, or staffing, so the launch order should be set by identity coverage and opt-in status, not by which channels appear.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Public pages can only show that a contact path is published. They cannot show whether submissions are answered, whether the address is monitored, or whether the visitor is authenticated. In consumer subscription support, the questions that justify an agent — plan changes, billing, account access — require identity the channel must already hold. A channel with verified identity and existing opt-in lets the agent act; a merely listed channel lets it only converse. Ranking by presence therefore systematically over-ranks the channels least able to resolve anything, and the team ships an agent that looks live but cannot close a ticket. The fix is an explicit scoring pass that treats 'documented' as one input and identity/consent as the gating inputs.
implementation_ideas: Build a channel inventory from public pages only, one row per contact path, with columns for identity coverage (verified / claimed / anonymous), consent status (existing opt-in / implied by initiation / none), and documented-versus-operated flag.
Score each row and sort; require any channel to clear an identity-and-consent threshold before it can be ranked first, regardless of how prominently it is published.
Re-verify the top two rows against internal analytics (submission volume, response ownership) and annotate the matrix with what public sources could not confirm.
identified_risks: Public pages may omit an operated channel entirely, producing a false negative in the inventory.
Team reads the matrix as a permanent ranking rather than a snapshot that decays as channels change.
identified_opportunities: The matrix doubles as the artifact that forces an owner and response-time commitment onto every listed channel.
Scoring exposes channels that are published but unowned, which is a cheap fix independent of the agent.

insights.insight: Consent is channel-specific and does not transfer: a web form submission is not an opt-in to an ongoing agent conversation, and an email address captured for receipts is not consent to proactive agent replies, so the team needs a per-channel consent map before the agent sends anything unprompted.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Each channel carries a different consent posture. A customer initiating inside a signed-in product has clearly invited a response in that session. A form submission invites a reply to that inquiry, not necessarily a continuing thread. A messaging opt-in is the strongest ongoing consent but only if a verified number or handle was captured with it. If the team treats one channel's consent as portable, the agent will send proactive messages on channels where consent was never collected, and the first symptom is unsubscribes or ignored threads. Mapping consent per channel, and defining what the agent may do at each consent level, keeps the agent inside the permission it actually has and makes the escalation path to human review explicit where consent is thin.
implementation_ideas: Write a consent map with one row per channel and three columns: what consent exists, what the agent may send under it, and what requires fresh opt-in.
Define a consent floor for proactive agent messages — verified identity plus recorded opt-in — and block proactive sends on any channel below the floor.
Attach the consent level to each conversation record so the agent's behavior and the human handoff both read from the same field.
identified_risks: Consent captured by a third-party form or tool may not be exportable, leaving the agent blind to it.
Overly strict floor suppresses useful follow-ups on channels where consent is implied but unrecorded.
identified_opportunities: A recorded consent field enables proactive follow-up on the strongest channel once the floor is met.
The map becomes reusable for any future channel without re-litigating consent from scratch.

insights.insight: Scope the agent's knowledge base to what each channel's identity can actually resolve; an agent on an anonymous channel should triage and route, not attempt account or billing resolution it cannot verify.
insights.supporting_reasoning: An agent's usefulness is bounded by what it can see. On a verified-identity channel it can read subscription state and resolve account questions end to end. On an anonymous public form it can answer pre-sale and general questions and route the rest, but any attempt at account resolution becomes a guessing game that erodes trust. Scoping the knowledge base per channel — full resolution set on the identity-verified channel, triage-and-route set on the anonymous one — keeps the agent honest about its limits and makes the escalation spec load-bearing rather than decorative. It also gives the team a clean way to expand scope as identity coverage improves on a channel, instead of rewriting the agent wholesale.
implementation_ideas: Split the knowledge base into a full-resolution set (identity-verified channels only) and a triage-and-route set (anonymous channels), with an explicit rule for which set each channel loads.
Write the escalation spec alongside the triage set so every routed question has a named destination and response-time owner.
Review the split monthly and promote questions from triage to full resolution only when the channel's identity coverage supports it.
identified_risks: Triage-only agents on anonymous channels feel shallow and may depress form completion.
Scope split drifts if the knowledge base is edited without re-checking channel identity coverage.
identified_opportunities: Honest scoping builds trust and reduces wrong-answer escalations.
The split creates a measurable path to widen scope as identity coverage grows.

experts.name: Bastian Kohl
experts.background: Builds cloud-agent configs with instruction sets, model selection, and feature toggles; experienced with sync-based config pipelines and scoped API credential issuance.
experts.lens: Whether a single agent config can be authored, versioned, and synced safely, and whether credentials and gateway settings are scoped to chat only.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com may not expose enough detail about Keiki's actual product surface (chat widget, embedded SDK, email, in-app messaging) to confirm which channels are truly supported versus merely marketed, so channel sequencing could rest on inference. A single agent config spanning multiple channels risks coupling: if channel-specific gateway settings and scoped API credentials are not isolated per channel, a config change for one channel can silently alter behavior or credential scope for another. Versioning is the core hazard: without an explicit config schema, environment separ
experts.opportunities: A chat-first launch keeps the credential and gateway surface smallest: one channel, one scoped credential, one gateway route, which is the easiest configuration to author, review, and roll back. Treating the agent config as a versioned artifact (schema-validated file, PR-reviewed, synced through a pipeline with staging-to-production promotion) turns launch into a repeatable, auditable process rather than a console-only setup. Feature toggles per channel let the team enable chat now and gate email or in-app channels behind flags without forking the config. Scoped, short-lived credentials issued
experts.recommendation: Launch on the single lowest-friction, most self-contained channel the public pages indicate Keiki supports (most likely an embedded web chat), and author the agent as one versioned, schema-validated config with per-channel feature toggles, environment-scoped gateway settings, and chat-only scoped credentials. Hold email and any in-app or third-party messaging channels behind disabled toggles until the chat config has passed review, staging sync, and rollback rehearsal. Required launch artifacts: the config file and its schema, an instruction set with eval cases, a model-selection rationale, a

insights.insight: Channel choice should be driven by credential and gateway isolation cost, not by reach; chat-first is the safest first channel because it needs the narrowest scoped credential and a single gateway route.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Each additional channel multiplies the config surface: separate gateway settings, separate credential scope, and separate failure modes. A chat surface can be served by one scoped, short-lived credential tied to a single route, so a leak or misconfiguration has a bounded blast radius and revocation is a single action. Email and third-party messaging typically require broader or longer-lived credentials and inbound parsing, which is harder to review and roll back. Starting with the channel that has the smallest credential footprint lets the team validate the authoring, versioning, and sync pipeline on the simplest case before adding channels behind toggles.
implementation_ideas: Define a per-channel credential scope table and mark chat as the only enabled scope at launch, with email and messaging scopes pre-declared but unissued.
Route all chat traffic through one gateway route per environment so gateway settings are isolated from future channels.
Add a launch gate that blocks enabling a second channel until the chat config has passed review, staging sync, and one rollback rehearsal.
identified_risks: Public pages may not confirm which channels Keiki actually supports, so the chat-first assumption could need revision.
Per-channel credential scoping may not be natively supported and could require a proxy layer.
identified_opportunities: Smallest credential surface at launch reduces incident blast radius.
A per-channel scope table becomes reusable documentation for later channel rollouts.

insights.insight: The agent config must be a versioned, schema-validated artifact synced through a pipeline with diff and rollback, not a console-only setup, or instruction sets, model selection, and toggles will drift between environments.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent changes often: instructions get tuned, models get swapped, toggles flip. If those edits happen only in a console, there is no reviewable diff, no reproducible staging state, and no clean rollback. Treating the config as a file with a schema catches malformed toggles and missing fields before sync, and a pipeline with approval and diff steps makes every production change auditable. This is the same discipline as infrastructure-as-code applied to agent configuration, and it is what makes a single config safe to sync across environments.
implementation_ideas: Author a JSON schema for the config covering instruction set, model selection, and toggle matrix, and validate in CI before any sync.
Implement a sync pipeline with staging-to-production promotion, a rendered diff on every change, and a one-step rollback to the last approved version.
Store the config in version control with required review on changes to instructions, model selection, and credential scope.
identified_risks: Schema churn early on can slow iteration if the schema is over-constrained.
Pipeline complexity may exceed what a small product team can maintain.
identified_opportunities: Reproducible staging state makes pre-launch testing meaningful.
Audit trail supports later compliance or incident review.

insights.insight: Credentials and gateway settings must be scoped to chat only and separated per environment, so the customer-facing surface never inherits account-level privilege.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent is the most exposed surface, so its credentials should carry only the permissions chat needs and should be short-lived and rotatable. If credentials are issued at account level or shared across environments, a staging misconfiguration can reach production resources and a leak grants more than chat requires. Gateway settings deserve the same treatment: per-environment routes and host allowlists keep staging traffic from hitting production endpoints. Scoping is cheap to design up front and expensive to retrofit once channels and environments share credentials.
implementation_ideas: Issue separate chat-scoped credentials per environment with short TTLs and a documented rotation runbook.
Configure gateway routes and host allowlists per environment so staging cannot reach production endpoints.
Add a pre-sync check that fails if a credential's scope exceeds chat or if an environment references another environment's gateway.
identified_risks: Short TTLs add rotation overhead and can cause outages if rotation is not automated.
Keiki's public pages may not document credential scoping, so the design may need adaptation to its actual model.
identified_opportunities: Routine revocation becomes a single action with bounded impact.
Environment isolation reduces staging-to-production accidents.

experts.name: Noor Haddad
experts.background: Designs product knowledge ingestion from docs, websites, and app APIs or MCP servers for customer-facing assistants; focuses on source freshness and grounding quality.
experts.lens: What knowledge sources must exist before launch and how to keep answers grounded rather than hallucinated.
experts.risks: Public pages alone cannot reveal Keiki's internal source-of-truth systems, so the team may assume the website is a sufficient knowledge base when the real answers live in app APIs, order systems, or support macros. Without a defined freshness contract, a customer-facing agent will confidently state stale pricing, availability, or policy details. Grounding quality also degrades if the agent must answer questions the public site never covers (order status, account issues, subscription changes), inviting hallucination or overreach. Channel-first sequencing risk: launching on high-expectation chan
experts.opportunities: Keiki's public site is a low-risk, high-signal corpus for a first launch: it establishes brand voice, product taxonomy, and the top-of-funnel questions customers actually ask. Starting on a narrow, low-stakes channel (a website help widget or FAQ-style assistant) lets the team validate retrieval precision, citation display, and escalation before touching transactional channels. A source registry with freshness SLAs and a 'grounded or escalate' policy turns grounding into a measurable product property rather than a hope. Public pages also give the team a clean baseline to diff against later API
experts.recommendation: Launch first on a single low-stakes, public-knowledge channel: an on-site help/FAQ assistant scoped strictly to content that exists on public Keiki pages, with every answer citing its source page and a hard fallback to human handoff when retrieval confidence is low. Before launch, the team must produce four artifacts: (1) a source registry listing each public page, its owner, canonical URL, and freshness SLA; (2) an ingestion pipeline with change detection and re-indexing on page updates; (3) a grounding contract defining answerable intents, citation requirements, and escalation triggers; (4)

insights.insight: The public Keiki site should be treated as the launch corpus, but only after it is inventoried into a source registry with freshness SLAs and canonical URLs.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent is only as grounded as its retrieval index. Public pages are the only knowledge the team can verify without internal access, so they are the correct starting corpus, but an uninventoried crawl mixes canonical pages with duplicates, outdated promos, and orphaned URLs. A registry forces each page to have an owner and a re-index trigger, which converts 'the site is our source' into an auditable contract. Without it, the agent cannot distinguish a current policy page from a superseded one, and grounding quality silently decays.
implementation_ideas: Build a source registry spreadsheet/table: URL, page type, owner, last-verified date, freshness SLA, and whether it is answer-eligible.
Add canonicalization and dedupe rules to the crawler so only canonical, answer-eligible pages enter the index.
Schedule automated change detection (hash diff on page content) that flags stale index entries and blocks answers from pages past their SLA.
identified_risks: Registry maintenance lapses and pages go unverified past SLA.
Marketing pages with time-bound claims get indexed and later misstate current offers.
identified_opportunities: Registry doubles as an audit trail for grounding quality reviews.
Freshness SLAs make hallucination measurable and regression-testable.

insights.insight: The first channel should be an on-site help/FAQ assistant, not in-app chat or email, because public-knowledge questions dominate what the launch corpus can actually ground.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Channel choice should follow retrieval coverage, not channel popularity. Public pages can ground product, brand, and general how-it-works questions; they cannot ground order status or account specifics without APIs. An on-site widget sets expectations low (help content) and keeps the blast radius small, while in-app chat and email raise expectations of transactional accuracy. Sequencing the widget first lets the team prove citation behavior and escalation before exposing the agent where a wrong answer is costlier.
implementation_ideas: Scope the widget to a defined intent list (product questions, general FAQ) and show a visible 'answers from our help pages' label with source links.
Instrument every answer with retrieval confidence and log low-confidence cases as escalation candidates for review.
Gate expansion to app APIs/in-app chat behind a grounding threshold (e.g., citation rate and hallucination score on the eval set).
identified_risks: Users ask transactional questions in the widget and get 'see your account' non-answers, eroding trust.
Scope creep pulls transactional intents in before APIs are wired.
identified_opportunities: Low-stakes channel produces clean grounding telemetry for tuning.
Visible citations build user trust and reduce support load on repetitive questions.

insights.insight: A written grounding contract with mandatory citations and explicit escalation triggers is the artifact that prevents hallucination more than any model choice.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Hallucination in customer-facing agents is usually a policy gap, not a model gap: the agent answers when it should say 'I don't know.' A grounding contract defines which intents are answerable, requires every answer to cite a retrieved source, and specifies fallback to human handoff on low retrieval confidence or uncovered intents. Paired with an evaluation set of real questions and expected source pages, it turns grounding into a testable property. Without it, the team cannot tell whether a fluent answer is grounded or invented.
implementation_ideas: Write the contract as a spec: answerable intents, required citation format, confidence threshold for fallback, and escalation routing.
Build an eval set of real customer questions with expected source pages and a hallucination scorecard run on every index or prompt change.
Enforce citation in the response layer: strip or flag answers whose claims lack a retrieved source span.
identified_risks: Over-strict thresholds cause excessive handoffs and a useless assistant.
Eval set drifts from real traffic if not refreshed from logged questions.
identified_opportunities: Contract and scorecard become reusable templates for later channels and API sources.
Escalation data reveals which APIs or pages to build next.

experts.name: Grady Whitlock
experts.background: Runs eval suites and trace-based QA for support agents; translates pricing-tier eval runs and logs into a pre-launch test plan with pass criteria.
experts.lens: What must be measured before go-live, and how logs and traces prove the agent behaves within its written boundaries.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com (a parenting/keiki-focused content and community site) suggest a consumer audience reached largely through content and community touchpoints, so the biggest evaluation risk is launching on a channel where the agent's written boundaries (scope of advice, escalation to humans, disclaimers) cannot be verified from logs before real users hit it. Without a defined trace schema, the team cannot prove the agent stays in-scope on parenting questions versus drifting into medical, legal, or product-recommendation territory. A second risk is that public pages alone do not rev
experts.opportunities: A narrow first channel lets the team build a trace-based QA harness cheaply: every conversation logged with intent, retrieved sources, boundary checks, and escalation events, then scored against a written rubric before widening exposure. Public content pages give a ready corpus for grounding and for drafting the agent's scope statement, which in turn becomes the source of testable pass criteria. A staged rollout (internal dogfood, then a low-traffic public surface, then the main channel) produces comparable eval runs across pricing-tier or model-tier configurations, so the team can choose a ti
experts.recommendation: Launch first on the lowest-blast-radius asynchronous channel Keiki already exposes publicly (contact/email or a single embedded chat widget on one content page), and gate go-live on an eval suite plus trace-based QA with written pass criteria: boundary adherence, correct escalation, grounded answers citing Keiki content, and no fabricated facts. Only promote to higher-traffic channels after a clean eval run and a sampled trace review at a defined threshold.

insights.insight: The agent's written boundaries must be converted into machine-checkable trace assertions before any channel goes live, because public pages alone cannot prove in-scope behavior.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Keiki's public surface is content and community oriented, so user questions will span parenting topics, site navigation, and adjacent advice. A boundary document is only real if each boundary maps to a loggable event: intent classification, source citations, escalation trigger, and refusal path. Trace-based QA turns those events into pass/fail checks, which is the only way to demonstrate the agent behaves within its written limits rather than asserting it does.
implementation_ideas: Define a trace schema capturing user intent, retrieved Keiki sources, boundary checks fired, escalation events, and final response, with a stable conversation ID.
Write a rubric mapping each boundary in the agent's scope doc to a specific trace assertion and a pass threshold.
Run a pre-launch eval suite of scripted and sampled conversations, scoring traces automatically and reviewing a human sample before sign-off.
identified_risks: Trace schema drift if the agent's scope doc changes without updating assertions.
Boundaries too vague to assert, producing false passes.
Logging gaps on channels that do not capture full threads.
identified_opportunities: Reusable eval harness for future channels and model tiers.
Boundary assertions double as regression tests after prompt changes.
Trace evidence supports a defensible go/no-go decision.

insights.insight: Channel choice should be driven by observability, not reach: the first channel must produce complete, reviewable traces at low public exposure.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Synchronous chat is high-signal but high-blast-radius; asynchronous contact channels are slower but fully logged and easy to sample. For a first launch, the team needs volume sufficient to score but small enough that failures are recoverable. A single embedded widget on one content page, or the existing contact path, gives complete threads, controlled traffic, and a clean rollback, whereas opening the main community surface first multiplies unlogged failure modes.
implementation_ideas: Rank candidate channels on a matrix of trace completeness, traffic controllability, and rollback ease, and pick the top scorer.
Instrument the chosen channel with full-thread logging and a kill switch before any public exposure.
Stage rollout: internal dogfood, then a capped-traffic public surface, then the main channel, with eval gates between stages.
identified_risks: Low-traffic channel yields too few traces to reach statistical comfort.
Channel-specific logging gaps mask failures.
Stakeholders push for the highest-reach channel prematurely.
identified_opportunities: Controlled first channel builds evidence for a confident wider launch.
Rollback ease reduces launch anxiety and speeds approval.
Channel matrix becomes a reusable decision artifact.

insights.insight: Pricing-tier and model-tier eval runs must be compared on the same trace suite so tier choice is evidence-based and boundary adherence is not traded away for cost.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Different model tiers will differ in grounding fidelity, escalation discipline, and refusal behavior, and those differences only surface under identical test conditions. Running the same scripted and sampled conversations across tiers, scored against the same rubric, isolates tier effects from channel or prompt effects. Without this, a cheaper tier can look adequate on happy paths while quietly eroding boundary adherence on edge cases.
implementation_ideas: Freeze one eval suite and rubric, then run every candidate tier against it unchanged.
Report per-tier pass rates on boundary adherence and escalation separately from answer quality.
Set a minimum boundary-adherence bar that any tier must clear before cost is considered.
identified_risks: Small suites overfit and misrank tiers.
Cost pressure overrides a failed boundary bar.
Tier changes invalidate prior trace baselines.
identified_opportunities: Defensible tier selection with documented evidence.
Rubric doubles as a regression gate for future tier changes.
Clear cost-versus-safety tradeoff for stakeholders.

experts.name: Ines Vukovic
experts.background: Writes job descriptions, tone guides, and escalation boundaries for customer-facing agents; pairs voice specs with channel-specific constraints.
experts.lens: Whether the agent's role, voice, and refusal/escalation rules are written down and testable before any channel is connected.
experts.risks: Public pages for onkeiki.com are thin on operational detail, so any channel decision rests on inferred positioning rather than documented capability. The core voice-and-scope risk: a product team connects a channel before the agent's role, tone, refusal rules, and escalation boundaries are written down and testable, meaning the first real customer conversation becomes the spec. Channel-specific constraints (synchronous chat vs. async email vs. voice) each impose different latency, turn-taking, and handoff expectations, and an unwritten voice guide will drift per channel. Without a named owner
experts.opportunities: Keiki's public positioning as a customer-facing agent product gives the team a natural framing for a written role charter before any integration. A narrow, low-stakes first channel (async, text-based) lets the team test refusal and escalation rules against real transcripts cheaply. Publishing the voice guide and escalation matrix as internal artifacts creates a reviewable baseline that survives team changes and makes later channel expansion a configuration exercise rather than a rewrite. Testable artifacts also let QA and support share one source of truth.
experts.recommendation: Launch first on a single asynchronous text channel (web chat or email-style messaging) and gate the launch on three written, testable artifacts completed before any channel is connected: (1) a role charter naming the agent's job, in-scope and out-of-scope tasks, and the human owner; (2) a tone guide with channel-specific constraints and do/don't examples; (3) an escalation boundary matrix listing refusal triggers, handoff conditions, and the exact handoff message. Treat synchronous voice and high-volume social channels as phase two, after transcripts from phase one validate the rules.

insights.insight: The role charter and escalation matrix must be written and testable before the first channel is connected, not after.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A customer-facing agent's behavior is only as good as its written boundaries; once a channel is live, every undocumented edge case becomes a de facto policy set by whichever engineer or prompt is closest. Writing the charter first converts voice and scope from tacit taste into reviewable criteria that QA, support, and product can all test against. This ordering also forces the team to name a human owner for escalations before customers can trigger them.
implementation_ideas: Draft a one-page role charter with explicit in-scope, out-of-scope, and 'always escalate' lists, signed off by product and support leads.
Build an escalation matrix mapping trigger conditions to handoff targets and exact handoff copy, with a test case per row.
Add a launch checklist gate: no channel credentials issued until charter, tone guide, and matrix pass review.
identified_risks: Charter written by one person without support input misses real escalation paths.
Gate slows launch and gets waived under deadline pressure.
identified_opportunities: Charter doubles as onboarding material for future agents and channels.
Testable matrix enables regression testing as prompts change.

insights.insight: Channel choice should be driven by constraint fit, not by volume; async text first, synchronous voice later.
insights.supporting_reasoning: Each channel imposes different constraints: async text tolerates drafting, review, and slower turns, while voice demands real-time turn-taking and exposes tone drift immediately. Starting async lets the team validate refusal and escalation rules against transcripts before adding latency pressure. Voice should follow only once the written rules have survived real traffic, because voice failures are harder to inspect after the fact.
implementation_ideas: Score candidate channels on a simple matrix: latency tolerance, transcript availability, handoff ease, and blast radius.
Pilot on the lowest-blast-radius async channel with a capped audience and weekly transcript review.
Define explicit exit criteria (e.g., refusal-rule pass rate on reviewed transcripts) before enabling voice.
identified_risks: Async-first may under-serve customers who expect instant answers.
Exit criteria set too loosely let voice launch prematurely.
identified_opportunities: Transcript review builds a labeled dataset for tuning.
Constraint matrix becomes reusable for every future channel.

insights.insight: The tone guide must be written per channel, with concrete examples, or voice will drift between channels.
insights.supporting_reasoning: A single generic tone guide collapses under channel constraints: brevity rules for chat contradict warmth rules for email, and voice needs spoken cadence guidance that text guides never cover. Concrete do/don't examples anchored to each channel make the guide testable rather than aspirational. Without this, the same agent sounds like different products depending on where the customer reaches it.
implementation_ideas: Write one core tone guide plus a short channel-constraint appendix per channel (length, formality, formatting, handoff phrasing).
Pair every tone rule with one good and one bad example drawn from drafted, not real, conversations.
Run a blind review where reviewers match sample replies to the correct channel and flag mismatches.
identified_risks: Per-channel appendices multiply maintenance as channels grow.
Examples can anchor too narrowly and stifle appropriate variation.
identified_opportunities: Channel appendices make expansion a documentation task, not a redesign.
Blind review gives a cheap, repeatable tone QA method.

debate.name: Mara Voss
debate.statement: I'll build on Nadia Okonkwo's readiness-score framing but tighten it: her scorecard ranks channels by identity, opt-in, and volume, yet volume alone can push the team toward a channel where identity and consent are thin. My sequencing rule is stricter — the launch channel must be the one where verified identity AND documented consent both already exist on a public-facing flow, with volume as a tiebreaker only. From public pages, Keiki's owned web surface (account creation, checkout, support entry points) is the only place where both can plausibly co-exist; messaging channels should stay held back until the primary channel clears explicit thresholds. To make that gate real rather than rhetorical, five artifacts are launch-blocking: an identity resolution map, a per-channel consent matrix, a narrow agent scope (order/account questions plus routing, with human handoff), a threshold sheet th

debate.name: Desmond Achebe
debate.statement: Mara, I agree with your sequencing logic — identity plus consent coverage should pick the channel, not ambition — but I'd tighten the artifact list before anyone ships. Your five artifacts are the right shape, yet they omit the thing that makes a first launch reversible: a versioned canonical config with a tested rollback to the previous pinned version. Identity resolution and a consent matrix tell us who we may talk to; they don't tell us how to un-ship a bad instruction set at 2am. My concrete amendment: keep your coverage audit and your five artifacts, and add a single canonical cloud-agent config (one versioned instruction set, pinned model, per-channel and per-capability toggles) plus a staging-to-prod sync pipeline and a rollback drill that must pass before the widget goes live. On channel choice, the public pages are the only evidence we have, so the owned web property is the defe

debate.name: Priya Raghunathan
debate.statement: I'll agree with Amara Chen, because her sequencing and her gate list are the same shape as mine, and she adds the one thing my own answer left implicit: the test script that exercises every refusal and escalation path before go-live. Where I'd push her is on 'highest-scriptability' as a selection criterion — scriptability is a property of the conversation design, not the channel, so it can quietly become an excuse to pick the surface the writer finds easiest rather than the one where Keiki's customers actually are. My launch-blocking trio stands: a written agent job description (does / does not / hands off), a tone guide with do/don't examples in Keiki's register including how to sound warm while uncertain, and an escalation boundary spec with named triggers, handoff copy, and a human owner — then a transcript review that runs the job description and boundaries against real support conve

debate.name: Tobias Lindqvist
debate.statement: I'll agree with Hana Sørensen and Noor Haddad, and push back on the identity-first camp (Mara Voss, Nadia Okonkwo, Corinne Adeyemi, Lena Okafor) on one point: on public evidence alone, we cannot confirm that Keiki has a signed-in surface with verified identity and documented consent, so sequencing on identity coverage risks stalling the launch on an unverified assumption. What we can verify from public pages is that Keiki publishes product and FAQ content, and that is the only corpus we can ground v1 against without guessing. So: launch on the public website help/FAQ surface with a strictly bounded public corpus, hard citation rules, and a deferral policy for anything touching pricing exceptions, account state, or commitments. The source registry, freshness SLA, and citation contract become the template every later channel inherits. Where I'd extend Hana and Noor: the registry should car

debate.name: Elena Marchetti
debate.statement: I'll respond to Mara Voss, because her sequencing logic is the closest to mine but stops one step short of the gate that actually matters. Mara says pick the channel with the highest coverage of verified identity and documented consent, then ship a narrow scope with human handoff. I agree with the selection criterion and the narrow scope, but coverage alone is not a launch gate — it's a ranking. My addition: whichever channel wins that ranking must also be the one with the best traceability, because the first channel exists to generate reviewable evidence, not just to serve customers. So the artifact set Mara lists (identity resolution map, per-channel consent matrix) needs to be paired with a written eval plan carrying numeric per-intent pass thresholds, a weekly trace-review cadence with named reviewers and sampling rules, and a signed go/no-go checklist. Without those, a channel can c

debate.name: Nadia Okonkwo
debate.statement: I'll respond to Corinne Adeyemi, because her sequencing rule is the closest to mine and the one place we diverge matters. Corinne says: answer first on the single channel with verified identity and existing opt-in, and explicitly do not launch on WhatsApp or iMessage first unless public pages show Keiki already collecting a messaging opt-in. I agree with the rule and the caution, and I'd tighten the evidence bar before anyone names a channel. From public pages alone we can see what Keiki publishes and what its site invites, but we cannot confirm verified identity or documented consent on any channel — those live in the product and the consent records, not the marketing site. So the first deliverable is not a channel pick, it's a channel readiness scorecard built from an actual inventory of public-facing flows (account creation, checkout, support entry points), scored on identity coverage

top5.title: Launch first on the owned public web/help surface, scoped to public-content questions only
top5.detail: Pick the single owned, public-facing web surface (on-site help/FAQ-style widget or contact-form assistant) as the v1 channel and scope the agent strictly to questions answerable from Keiki's own published pages. Explicitly exclude anything transactional or account-specific at v1, with a hard human handoff. Hold email, in-app, and any messaging channel behind a toggle until the first channel has a clean transcript review and a rollback drill. The channel decision stays provisional until someone inventories the live product to confirm whether a signed-in help surface actually exists.
top5.rationale: The debate converged on the public web surface as the only channel defensible on public evidence: it is the one surface where Keiki controls both the source of truth and freshness, and it needs no unverified messaging opt-in. Tobias, Hana, and Noor anchored this on grounding discipline; Sofia and Grady added the low-blast-radius, read-mostly framing; Bastian and Rafael supplied the engineering posture of one versioned config with toggles. The identity-first camp's objection is real but is a ranking concern, not a blocker, because v1 scope excludes account-specific answers.

top5.title: Make a source-of-truth registry and citation contract launch-blocking
top5.detail: Before any session, build a source registry mapping each public page or doc to an owner, canonical URL, and freshness SLA, plus a crawl-and-index pipeline with change detection and re-index triggers. skills.instructions:
# Keiki Public-Web Agent Launch Scope

## Overview
Defines the v1 channel decision and scope contract for a customer-facing agent on Keiki's owned, public-facing web surface (on-site help/FAQ-style widget or contact-form assistant). The agent answers only questions answerable from Keiki's own published pages; anything transactional or account-specific is out of scope at v1 and routed to a human. Based on public pages only; not a commissioned engagement.

## When to use
- The team must pick the single first channel for the agent.
- Scope, exclusions, and handoff behavior need to be written and signed off before build.
- A reviewer asks "what does v1 answer, and what does it refuse?"

## Inputs
- List of Keiki's public pages and help/FAQ URLs (public only).
- Candidate owned surfaces (help widget vs. contact-form assistant).
- Named human owner and handoff destination (email/form/queue).

## Steps
1. Inventory owned, public-facing surfaces; pick exactly one as v1. Prefer the surface with the most public-content traffic and lowest account dependency.
2. Write the in-scope intent list: only questions answerable from published pages.
3. Write the out-of-scope list: pricing quotes, orders, accounts, refunds, anything requiring login.
4. Define the hard human handoff: trigger conditions, handoff message, destination, and SLA owner.
5. Define refusal wording for out-of-scope questions (see `scope-checklist.md`).
6. Record the decision, owner, and date in the config repo; mark launch-blocking.
7. Re-review scope whenever a new page type or channel is proposed.

## Output format
A filled `scope-checklist.md` plus a one-paragraph channel decision record (surface, rationale, owner, date).

## Guardrails
- One channel only at v1; no email, in-app, or social DMs.
- No transactional or account-specific answers, even if the model "knows" them.
- Every out-of-scope question must end in a handoff, never a guess.
- Cite only public Keiki pages; do not invent customers, metrics, or quotes.

## Example
Input: help widget vs. contact form. Decision: contact-form assistant, because it is public, low-risk, and already collects handoff details. In scope: "how does Keiki work", "where do I find X feature". Out of scope: "what will my plan cost", "where is my order" → handoff to support form with a summary.

skills.instructions:
# Keiki Source Registry and Citation Contract

## Overview
Creates the source registry and crawl/index pipeline that make grounded answers possible, plus a citation-required answer contract. Every public page or doc maps to an owner, canonical URL, and freshness SLA; every answer links its source. Public sources only.

## When to use
- Before the first agent session, to establish the knowledge base.
- When a page changes, is added, or goes stale.
- When auditing whether answers are grounded.

## Inputs
- Public page URLs from onkeiki.com and public help/FAQ pages.
- Page owners and review cadence.
- Index store and change-detection tooling.

## Steps
1. Crawl public pages; record canonical URL, title, owner, and last-verified date per entry using `registry-schema.json`.
2. Assign a freshness SLA per page type (e.g., help articles vs. marketing pages).
3. Stand up change detection; on diff, flag the entry and trigger re-index or owner review.
4. Index only registry-approved pages; block unregistered URLs from retrieval.
5. Enforce the citation contract: every answer includes the canonical URL of each source used.
6. If no registered source supports an answer, the agent says so and offers handoff.
7. Run a weekly staleness report; expired entries drop from retrieval until re-verified.

## Output format
A populated registry conforming to `registry-schema.json`, plus a citation block appended to every answer.

## Guardrails
- No answer without a registered, in-SLA source.
- Canonical URL only; no mirrors or cached copies in citations.
- Stale entries are excluded, not silently used.
- Public pages only; no internal docs at v1.

## Example
Entry: `{ "url": "https://onkeiki.com/help/how-it-works", "owner": "content", "sla_days": 30, "last_verified": "2025-01-10" }`. Answer: "Keiki works by … (source: https://onkeiki.com/help/how-it-works)."

## Overview
Ships the agent as a single canonical config in version control (versioned instructions with changelog, pinned model, feature toggles, env-scoped gateway, chat-only scoped credentials) and gates go-live on a written eval plan with numeric thresholds and sampled trace review. Public sources only.
